💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past.
  • During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.
  • The finds began piling up in the spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, digging under Calle Hilera, a busy street in Málaga, Spain, is bound to churn up remnants of the seaside city’s past. Officials just didn’t expect those remnants to be the literal remains of more than 1,000 people from the Roman era.

During a project to extend the local metro line toward a future hospital site, crews exposed 984 burial complexes holding the remains of more than 1,000 people, according to the regional ministry of public works, as reported by Sur.

The finds began piling up in the spring. When the discovery was first confirmed, the metro authority had uncovered 600 burials. Since then, the count has climbed past 1,000 individuals, and officials expect it to keep rising. So far, investigations have revealed a wide variety of burial types, but all of them date from the second to fourth centuries C.E., when the Romans were dominant along the Iberian Peninsula’s coastline.

Industry observers note that although the crews found relatively few grave goods (mainly the expected pottery, coins, and a smattering of personal items), the necropolis, which stretches roughly 1,300 feet, has proven rich in other ways. Mario Muñoz-Atanet, the regional government’s public works delegate in Málaga, told Sur that the number of graves will likely grow as excavations continue.

The burials include tile-lined tombs, table-style tombs, and a range of simple pits. In a few cases, newborns were buried inside amphorae. Many graves were also reused. “We are working on them one by one, tomb by tomb,” Muñoz-Atanet remarked. “One tomb of each type will be displayed in the future metro archaeology museum.”.

According to Muñoz-Atanet, intends for that museum are already underway, and finds from the metro excavations will form the centerpiece of its collection.

It has been revealed that the burial site also lies close to where the Nasrid Wall was discovered. That wall was built by the Nasrid dynasty, which ruled the last Islamic kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula from the 13th to the 15th centuries, long after the Roman-era burials. Experts believe that in the second century, the necropolis sat well outside the city but along a key coastal route leading out of the urban center. The site may even have been underwater in the centuries before it became a burial ground.

According to recent reports, the excavations have also turned up coins from many different places. According to Muñoz-Atanet, these coins help confirm Málaga’s history as a port that drew people from all over.

That cosmopolitan past is no surprise. Málaga has passed through the hands of many rulers, and the modern city is built atop Phoenician, Roman, and Moorish settlements. Impressive historical finds are nothing newly introduced in the region. In 2005, for example, excavations at the Dolmen of Menga, a Neolithic monument in nearby Antequera that is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, shed light on the site’s ritual uses. A recent study found that the monument was still in use as recently as 1,000 years ago, which may rewrite its history.

If the past is any guide, Málaga’s next great discovery may be just one excavation away.

  • It has been revealed that we’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December.
  • But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa.
  • Recent findings suggest that in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’ll never forget the first time we visited Newly introduced York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Sources indicate that based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

In a recent development, december is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

According to recent reports, why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

Industry observers note that we’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

Sources indicate that we were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

It has been revealed that while Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sources indicate that sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like Upcoming York City at Christmas.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

Recent findings suggest that we’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

Sources indicate that we’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

It has been revealed that why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

It has been revealed that walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A Latest Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

It has been revealed that we went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

Sources indicate that we’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

Recent findings suggest that one of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Sources indicate that why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

In a recent development, why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Industry observers note that why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

According to recent reports, this was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Recent findings suggest that why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

Industry observers note that for the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Massive Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

It has been revealed that december is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have teamed up to solve the whodunit: 8,000 dead frogs discovered nearly a decade ago in a single ditch in Cambridgeshire, England.
  • In a recent development, the questions began between 2016 and 2018, when work on the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme uncovered a ditch filled with amphibian bones.
  • After studying the odd cold case, zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth and Vicki Ewens, senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, published their findings in Environmental Archaeology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scientists at Bournemouth University and the Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) have teamed up to solve the whodunit: 8,000 dead frogs discovered nearly a decade ago in a single ditch in Cambridgeshire, England. The twist? The frogs had been dead for 1,700 years. The scientists have put the mystery to rest by pinning the blame on a group of hungry short-eared owls. Reaching that conclusion, though, doesn’t clear every suspect in the case.

In a recent development, the questions began between 2016 and 2018, when work on the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme uncovered a ditch filled with amphibian bones. Radiocarbon dating by the University of Vienna placed the frogs in the Roman era. Experts then used a upcoming method of analysis to measure the frogs’ arm bones, which indicated that most of the frogs died young. They were eaten in the winter of their first year.

After studying the odd cold case, zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth and Vicki Ewens, senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, published their findings in Environmental Archaeology. Clarkson first compared the damage on the bones with earlier studies of predation and found that birds of prey had likely eaten the frogs. He named short-eared owls and hen harriers as the most likely suspects.

Recent findings suggest that on-site archaeological evidence added a twist, however: the ditch had filled within a single year. How could so many bones pile up so rapidly? The research team found that the waters of the surrounding marshy wetlands, including the ditch in question, were retreating during the Roman period. This created ideal breeding conditions for frogs, and more frogs meant more food for predatory birds.

“We suggest natural and anthropogenic environmental changes to explain why this predation occurred in the Middle Roman period,” the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that people also changed the landscape. The valley had been heavily wooded during the Iron Age, but snail, pollen, and charcoal evidence indicated major changes by the time of the frog massacre. Over time, farmers had cleared large areas of woodland to make grazing land for livestock. This left the frogs with less cover and drew in short-eared owls, which hunt over open grassland.

Sources indicate that “We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” Clarkson noted in a statement from the university. “The mystery of these frogs has been solved—a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls.”.

Industry observers note that the owls may not have dined alone, though. Clarkson called the die-off a “short, intensive predation event” that could have drawn a mix of predators, which also fed on shrews, mice, and voles. “Results showed this was the debris left by a community of predators,” the authors wrote.

Human activity may have helped the predators, too. Although people cut down trees to make room for livestock, the researchers mentioned that both the people and their animals were probably elsewhere during winter. That would have made it easier for the owls to roost near the ditch.

In the university’s statement, Ewens noted she had “so many theories” about why such a large collection of frog bones turned up there. Working together to answer the question, she added, shows how research on “even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

Clarkson agreed. “These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world—what wild animals were getting up to in the past,” he said, “and what life was like for them.”.

The Sanctuary of a Healing God Was Lost for 1,800 Years. Archaeologists May Have Finally Found It.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus.
  • Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.
  • Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus. The only issue: Nobody knew the location. But now, a scholar at the University of Athens thinks there’s enough evidence to claim we’ve solved the 1,800-year-old mystery.

Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.

Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city. Lambrinoudakis collated the research, noting that not only has he likely found the mystery location, but that cult worship of Asclepius took place at the site for longer than we knew about.

Recent findings suggest that the oldest religious building in Epidaurus—dated to around 600 B.C.E.—features a structure with an underground chamber cut directly into the bedrock, likely part of early healing traditions. In Greek mythology, Asclepius took over his father Apollo’s role as a healer, and Epione was worshiped for her ability to help soothe pain. The ancient structure has a pebble-lined floor, walls coated in dark red plaster, and a circular basin built into the floor accessible by staircase. The bottoms of four amphorae are embedded in the bedrock floor. In the fourth century B.C.E., crews built a new circular building directly to the west, likely a “deliberate continuity of the same chthonic cult of Asclepius,” the university wrote in a translated statement.

In a recent development, nearby, the teams found a ground-level altar made of limestone blocks that they believe is older than both buildings. Lambrinoudakis said the combination of the finds shows the cult likely dates to the seventh century B.C.E.

Sources indicate that the structure served as a key gathering point in Epidaurus. Excavations revealed walls that created a processional route to and from the building, essentially an uncovered passageway for visitors. A large square in the center of the sanctuary features open space in front of the temple, a key functional element of the site.

“It could accommodate the throngs of pilgrims who arrived at the site to take part in the sacrificial offering to Asclepius, which was accompanied by a festive procession,” the university wrote. To the east, an altar and platforms included seating for prominent families who watched the sacrificial rituals.

In a recent development, beneath Building K, excavators found an earlier structure from the early third century B.C.E. that sat on an unusually sturdy limestone foundation. The Roman building on top of it, which was rebuilt several times between the second and late fourth centuries C.E., has a central courtyard that probably had colonnades on at least three sides. The courtyard also has a gravel floor and a small basin made from reused marble pieces. In the building’s southwest corner, a large hall with a small basin or bath and a round room resembles spaces in other Epidaurus buildings that have been linked to the worship of Egyptian gods.

According to recent reports, in the northwest corner of Building K, on a lower level, sits an unusual, nearly intact crypt that opens to the north. Along its west side, reused column pieces from an unknown earlier building form a three-part niche, and gaps in the wall behind it let sunlight stream in at midday. “The overall character of ‘K’ suggests that it may have been the site of a mystical cult, particularly during the late Roman period,” the university said, adding they were unable to define who—or what—the cult worshipped.

In the agora of ancient Epidaurus, just northwest of the city’s small theater, excavators had already uncovered a monumental fourth-century B.C.E. fountain complex. More recently, they found a large walled enclosure right next to it. Inside were small clay offerings that may once have hung from trees, a piece of a clay heating vessel, and a pottery fragment scratched with part of Asclepius’s name.

At the center of the enclosure, a well fed an underground pointed-arch tunnel that carried water to the fountain. Because water was central to the worship of Asclepius, the university says the offerings, the well, and the fountain together identify the site as the long-lost town sanctuary Pausanias described. Excavators also found a larger-than-life marble statue of a woman in the enclosure. Lambrinoudakis thinks it may be the statue of Epione that Pausanias saw, but without an inscription, he can’t be sure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.
  • Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond swiftly to cybersecurity and other threats.
  • The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with fresh risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond swiftly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with fresh risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

Industry observers note that the legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

Recent findings suggest that “With advances in AI creating fresh cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster stated in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”.

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI concerns on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

According to recent reports, he has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking noted.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

Recent findings suggest that in his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

According to recent reports, he's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

Recent findings suggest that “He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking mentioned. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

According to recent reports, the software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary indicates.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You can’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs, and you can’t complete a project at home or in your workshop without making a mess. These are the laws of the universe. I don’t write them; I just obey them.

In a recent development, but because of this, I also know the importance of a reliable shop vac. Unlike the vacuum you use to clean the floors in your home, a shop vac gobbles up large, chunky messes, including sawdust, screws, bits of wood, and other debris (not to mention spills and other wet messes). So if you’re using woodworking tools like sanders, miter saws, and table saws on a regular basis, you need to have one close by.

When it comes to choosing the right shop vac for your home, there’s a lot to consider. Shop vacs come in both cordless and corded electric models and range in size from small, 1.6-gallon portable vacuums for cleaning out cars to large, 12-gallon shop vacs capable of keeping your entire garage sawdust-free.

All of the products written about below were tested by members of the Popular Mechanics team, including myself (Tony Carrick) and Test Editor Brad Ford.

Recent findings suggest that in an effort to evaluate the performance of the shop vacs on this list, we put them through tests that involved collecting both dry materials and liquid. We conducted three timed tests using only each vacuum’s hose, no attachments. The first test involved vacuuming up 12 cups of sawdust to determine how rapidly each vac could collect dry material. We then used each vac to drain 2 gallons of water from a bucket. Lastly, we tested suction power by attempting to use each vac to suck up wood screws and metal bolts.

Along with grading each shop vac’s vacuuming capabilities, we also evaluated how easy each model was to use, based on factors like weight, size, capacity, and cord and hose length. Since every person’s shop vac needs may vary, the list below includes a broad range of sizes.

Recent findings suggest that in the latest update of this guide, we tested and added two latest shop vacs. The Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+ is a shop vac with next-level features you won’t find on any other shop vacs. Not only does it connect to the exhaust ports of the large sawdust-producing power tools in your workshop, table saws, miter saws, and the like, but it also syncs with them via a wireless remote. With a vacuum cleaner–like dust collection bag and top-mounted HEPA filter, it’s ideally equipped for collecting sawdust.

Recent findings suggest that the Craftsman CMXEVBE17595 Wet-Dry Shop Vac is our largest pick (with its 16-gallon tank) and also one of our most powerful. With a max airflow of 185 cubic feet per minute (cfm), it sucks up material faster than any other shop vac we tested. It’s also powerful enough to pull in heavier objects, including bolts and small chunks of wood.

The Vacmaster’s impressive power and compact design make it the perfect all-around shop vac. One of our editors owns the previous iteration of this model and has found it to be the ideal shop vac for home use. Its 5.5-hp motor is much more powerful than what you’ll find with most other 5-gallon shop vacs. It also has a small, 18.6-by-13.4-inch footprint, so it’s easy to carry and store, though its smaller capacity may not be enough for busier workshops.

Sources indicate that with an 18-foot power cord and 7-foot hose, you won’t need an extension cord to clean up a large two-car garage or reach a car in the driveway. Plus, the newest version of the Vacmaster adds wheels that make it even easier to move around. There are also four attachments, which offer enough versatility to handle different jobs, and all of the Vacmaster’s attachments fit neatly into a storage compartment on the vacuum.

Full Vacmaster Beast Series 5-Gallon Shop Vacuum Review.

Stanley’s 6-gallon wet-dry vac is a fraction of the cost of other shop vacs, yet it still packs enough power and capacity to handle most cleanups. Though it lagged behind the top performers we tested, it still completed our sawdust test in a respectable 21 seconds, and it swallowed up 2 gallons of water in just 11 seconds. And with its smaller-diameter hose, it produced enough suction to pick up both screws and bolts.

It’s not too bulky, so it won’t crowd your workshop floor, nor is it so compact that it requires emptying too frequently. It sits on swiveling casters and is relatively light, which made it easy to wheel around our tester’s garage. We also liked its accessories, which include two extensions and three nozzles for both floor and spill cleanup. The crevice tool was particularly impressive in that it reached easily into the tight spaces between the seats of one of our cars.

Industry observers note that we did find ourselves wishing the power cord was longer than 10 feet so we could reach all corners of the workshop without having to use an extension cord. Still, with its low price and ample capacity, this Stanley vac is a great value option for any home workshop.

Ridgid's shop vac is powerful and affordable enough to fit most budgets, making it an ideal companion for those bigger and messier home improvement projects.

Recent findings suggest that during testing, it collected a pile of sawdust in just over 16 seconds before proceeding to drain a bucket of water in about 6 seconds. While we liked how quickly it picked up light debris, the Ridgid left a little to be desired with lift power. Its large-diameter hose made quick work of lighter material, but it struggled to pick up larger bolts (though we should note that this was an problem with most other vacs with large 2-1/2-inch-diameter hoses).

Industry observers note that the Ridgid also has a sturdy feel to it. The hose resisted cracking or denting, even after mistakenly stepping on it, and the tub is made of thick plastic. There’s also a locking system on the hose, which prevents attachments from falling off when the vacuum is in use.

The vacuum’s long, 7-foot hose made it easy to clean a work area without having to repeatedly reposition the base. Attachments include two extension wands, along with a crevice tool and floor tool, all of which fit onto the shop vac for storage. An included wet filter would make this shop vac a real no-brainer purchase, but it’s not far off from that even without one.

Full Ridgid 12-Gallon 5.0 Peak HP NXT Shop Vacuum Review.

The speed and capacity the DeWalt Stealthsonic displayed during my tests makes it a great choice for cleaning up wet messes.

It produced some of the most impressive vacuuming results during our tests. Backed by its 5.5-hp motor and 2.5-inch-diameter hose (about the same size as a fire hose), the Stealthsonic gobbled up our pile of sawdust in just 16 seconds and drained our bucket of water in just 5 seconds, which was among the fastest of any shop vac we tested.

In a recent development, it was also one of the largest of the shop vacs we tested, with a 12-gallon capacity. Thanks to its 20-foot-long cord, it covers an entire two-car garage without the need for an extension cord, and it sits on heavy-duty rubber casters that make it easy to wheel around.

While its larger-diameter hose worked well for the quick collection of lighter materials, it’s not ideal for heavier objects. The Stealthsonic struggled to produce enough lift to suck up wood screws and was unable to collect larger bolts like some shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses could. It also is a bit too bulky to get into tighter spots, such as the small gaps in and around the seats in a car. But if you’re looking for something that rapidly cleans up larger spills and messes at the job site or in a workshop, this vacuum is it.

Milwaukee’s M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum, which runs off an 18-volt lithium-ion battery, is one of the most powerful shop vac options when there’s no electrical outlet in range. The vac impressed during testing, even matching some of the corded shop vacs we tested. It consumed our sawdust pile in 20 seconds flat and a bucket of water in just 11 seconds, which is saying something given that it has a long, 9-foot hose.

Sources indicate that we also loved the design of this wet-dry vac. The accessories, which include a floor utility nozzle and crevice tool, fit nicely inside a compartment on the top of the shop vac, and the tray holds both extensions. The extra-long hose and the small profile of the crevice tool were particularly valuable when we used the M18 Fuel wet-dry vacuum to clean out a car.

Sources indicate that the M18 6-gallon vacuum is also easy to maneuver. It sits in a sturdy tray with four casters with rubber wheels that rolled easily over our tester’s garage floor and driveway. The M18’s run time was also impressive. When loaded with a 12.0-ampere-hour (Ah) battery, we got 31 minutes of run time when set to high and a whopping 48 minutes on its lower power setting.

This was the priciest wet-dry vacuum we tested, but it’s worth the investment if you want to cut the cord without compromising power.

If the primary demand for your shop vac is to collect the mountains of sawdust left behind following a carpentry project, then look no further than the recently introduced Vacmaster Professional Beast Series FLT+. Not only will this shop vac attach to your power tools’ exhaust ports, but it also synchronizes with them. It comes with a Synchro key remote, which you attach to a power tool via a neoprene strap. The key communicates wirelessly with the shop vac. When it senses the vibration of the tool turning on, the key sends a signal that turns on the vacuum, eliminating the need to walk across the room to turn it on manually. I used it with a table saw, and it worked well, reliably turning on as soon as I fired up the table saw and dutifully sucking up dust as I cut, then turning off when I shut down the saw.

Industry observers note that the Vacmaster is designed for collecting dust particles, and it did that extremely well. It sucked up 12 cups of sawdust in under 20 seconds, which is impressive given that it comes equipped with a smaller 1-7/8-inch-diameter hose. The Vacmaster Beast FLT+ also comes with a dust bag similar to a vacuum cleaner and a HEPA filter, making it ideal for trapping fine dust particles.

Sources indicate that while most shop vacs have a filter located inside the collection tank, the Vacmaster’s is on top. This frees up space inside the tank for more debris collection while also preventing the filter from becoming inundated with dust. Other notable features you won’t find on most shop vacs include an LED display that reveals the vacuum's airflow percentage, so you know when it’s time to clean the filter, and a self-cleaning filter. It’s an excellent workshop shop vac for those who don’t mind springing for it.

It has been revealed that with its cordless design, light weight, and compact, box-shaped design, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac is made for the road. At just 15 inches long, 13 inches wide, and 12 inches high, and with a weight of just under 10 pounds, Milwaukee’s M12 Fuel shop vac was by far the easiest to carry around of the wet-dry vacuums we tested. Its shape also made it ideal for sitting in the trunk of a car or storing on a set of garage shelves.

It has been revealed that per its name, the M12 Fuel shop vac uses a smaller power source—a 12-volt battery—so it doesn’t have the power of the corded and 18-volt cordless models we tested. Still, it took a respectable 35 seconds for it to complete our sawdust test and was capable of sucking down both bolts and wood screws. Its 1.6-gallon capacity and a max runtime of 26 minutes on low and 14 minutes on high limit it to small cleanup jobs, however.

Sources indicate that while it lacks the power of larger shop vacs, it’s hard to overstate how convenient it is to use. We appreciated its compact size and cordless design when we toted it into the car for some detailing, then later up to a second-floor bonus room to clean up drywall dust after mounting a TV.

The M12 Fuel is pricey when you factor in the cost of a battery and charger, but its convenience is unmatched, especially if you’ve already bought into Milwaukee’s 12-volt power tool universe and have a 12-volt Fuel battery to load into it.

Full Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Shop Vac Review.

In a recent development, the Craftsman 16-gallon wet-dry shop vac was built to clean up large masses fast with a max airflow of 185 cfm, well above the 100 cfm I see on most shop vacs. It vacuumed up 12 cups of sawdust faster than any other shop vac I tested and gulped down 2 gallons of water in 5 seconds flat. Most of the shop vacs I tested with a larger 2-1/2-inch-diameter hose struggled to generate enough lift to pick up heavier debris. That wasn’t the case with the Craftsman, which effortlessly vacuumed up a pile of screws, washers, and large bolts.

The Craftsman sits on four sturdy casters that made it easy to maneuver around when I was using it to clean up my large two-car garage, which I was able to do thanks to its 20-foot-long power cord and 7-foot hose.

With its 16-gallon size, the Craftsman was also the largest shop vac I tested, which made it handy for cleaning up big messes and large open areas. It was less effective for cleaning out a car. The crevice tool and its bulkier hose made it difficult to maneuver around a car interior, and there are no crevice tools for cleaning the gaps between seats and other tight spaces.

While its large size makes the Craftsman capable of cleaning up large messes, it also makes it a bit of a space hog in a garage or shed. You also won’t be carrying it inside the house to clean up messes in the home. But if you’re after a shop vac with the muscle and capacity to handle large postproject messes, this is the one.

According to recent reports, the drum capacity of a shop vac determines how much material you can vacuum without having to empty it out. While sizes range from 1.6 to 16 gallons, smaller-capacity shop vacs, like the Milwaukee M12 Fuel 1.6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, provide more versatility to the average user through easier transport and storage. If you’re short on space, a smaller unit that you have to empty more frequently could be more convenient than a larger-capacity machine cluttering up your garage. Keep in mind that the stated gallon capacity doesn't factor in the space taken up by the filter, so don’t expect a 6-gallon model to suck up exactly 6 gallons of material.

While the majority of shop vacs use corded power, cordless models are becoming more common. These battery-powered options offer more mobility—especially useful for car, boat, or RV cleaning—but they lack the runtime for extended projects. If you prefer the mobility of cordless models (especially if you’re interested in a larger-capacity model that requires a lot of power), choose one from the same brand as your existing power tools. This enables you to extend runtime by using additional batteries you already have on hand.

If you decide to go with a corded model, pay attention to the length of the cord. Models with a longer cord, such as the DeWalt Stealthsonic Wet-Dry Shop Vacuum, give you the freedom to cover larger workshops or reach to your driveway without having to get out an extension cord.

Industry observers note that A shop vac’s airflow—measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm)—represents the amount of air a vacuum pulls through its nozzle. Roughly speaking, a shop vac with a higher cfm sucks up material faster than one with a lower cfm, though keep in mind this doesn’t include other factors like nozzle design, motor size, and suction power. As we found during testing, shop vacs with smaller-diameter hoses, such as the Milwaukee M18 Fuel 6-Gallon Wet-Dry Vacuum, often produce greater suction power. So while a larger shop vac with a larger-diameter hose will remove lightweight material, such as sawdust, more rapidly than a shop vac with a narrower hose, that smaller vac is better able to pick up heavier objects, such as bolts and coins.

Sources indicate that while most shop vacs include several nozzle attachments for the hose, some models offer a more useful variety of accessories. Think about the type and scope of your cleaning tasks, and look for a vacuum with applicable accessories. For example, we’ve found a brush-tip nozzle to be essential for automotive interior cleaning, allowing us to quickly clean dust and pet hair from the dashboard and display screen—areas easily scratched by a hard plastic nozzle. Or, if you want to suck up the cobwebs in the corner of your garage or sawdust deep under your workbench, look for vacs with multiple extension wands to extend the nozzle reach.

Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

📅 14 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.
  • Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”.
  • That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”.

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

Recent findings suggest that baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

According to recent reports, we have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In a recent development, in 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

In a recent development, this may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

According to recent reports, that is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger problem is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

Sources indicate that that is true in Toronto. It is true in Newly introduced York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

It has been revealed that international travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

Recent findings suggest that the Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Sources indicate that do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

According to recent reports, yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

This video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

Industry observers note that this matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that notes this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Recent findings suggest that make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Industry observers note that air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

According to recent reports, keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

Recent findings suggest that that receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The notable thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

It has been revealed that trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

Industry observers note that we use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag swiftly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

Sources indicate that but do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that states, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”.

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Recent findings suggest that never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Industry observers note that check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

We have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Sources indicate that not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

According to recent reports, the point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

In a recent development, that’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

That is usually fine — until it is not.

Sources indicate that so before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

In a recent development, the goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.
