#30691. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (929 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.
  • House Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment.
  • “The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” mentioned Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Industry observers note that republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

Recent findings suggest that fresh maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, stated he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

In a recent development, advocates for a latest map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley stated he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Industry observers note that democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Fresh York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for latest maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass latest maps and could decide to revisit the concern. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

Industry observers note that in Fresh Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

It has been revealed that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their fresh majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to latest maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

#30690. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (957 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Godsavethepoints ↗ Open Full Page

What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight.
  • Recent findings suggest that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about.
  • More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

Recent findings suggest that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

It has been revealed that even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

Recent findings suggest that it makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to rapidly reset and refresh before carrying on.

According to recent reports, the first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

In a recent development, as I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

It has been revealed that and this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

It has been revealed that now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

It has been revealed that in response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

Sources indicate that that’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The massive question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.
  • A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.
  • It has been revealed that massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie unveiled his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

Sources indicate that if the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie remarked he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

According to recent reports, he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie remarked some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

Sources indicate that "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie stated. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, noted on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Industry observers note that hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries stated. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The Fresh Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Industry observers note that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

Recent findings suggest that "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

It has been revealed that also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

In a recent development, massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s upcoming resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

📅 02 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes.
  • Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep.
  • Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a newly introduced card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To quell this matter, the fresh card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

It has been revealed that this model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

In a recent development, consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
  • “There were a lot of pins and needles,” noted Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” noted Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

It has been revealed that democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ mentioned David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

Sources indicate that but the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

It has been revealed that “In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

It has been revealed that the repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, stated redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye stated. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic challenges. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

According to recent reports, “There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

Womack mentioned her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

Sources indicate that “There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” remarked Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

Sources indicate that american Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis remarked. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he stated in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a upcoming map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he mentioned. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as key, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

It has been revealed that heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief commercial officer of the world’s largest airline remarked the carrier is positioning itself to be a “premium” option at the global level.

Speaking at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York on Thursday, American CCO Nat Pieper noted the airline is investing in and improving its highest leverage points.

It has been revealed that “That is an ongoing effort. So many different steps to the travel process. But I think we’ve made good progress. I feel like we’ve got momentum and we’re optimistic about where we’re going,” he mentioned.

Customer experience, loyalty, network strength, and premium products will be leading priorities, he added, since they encourage customers to stick with the airline over time.

Pieper also said the airline is focusing on optimizing operations at LAX.

Recent findings suggest that “Local yields are better than connecting traffic. If you’re going to win and jump on markets, you’ve got to focus on the local market. That’s what we’re going to do in Los Angeles,” he noted.

“It’s going to be a gradual build as we get to the end of ’28, when T4 and T5 will be ready to roll, we’ll have 30 gates there,” he continued. Terminal 4 and 5 are undergoing an extensive $1.6 billion modernization.

When it comes to the financials, Pieper remarked the best way to maximize cash flow is to invest in the product.

“The ultimate goal for American is generate as much cash flow as we can… You can pay your balance sheet and get it into the shape that you want it, as well as generate enough cash to be able to reinvest in your product and have people continue to want to fly your airline,” he said.

Industry News: A 500-Mile Kayak Journey Down the Congo River Went Viral—and Is Sparking a Bigger Conversation

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last month the Welsh adventurer and self-described extreme athlete Ash Dykes was paddling along the placid waters of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River flowing through Cameroon, Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo, when something stirred underneath his vessel, kicking up bubbles.
  • In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.
  • It has been revealed that when Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last month the Welsh adventurer and self-described extreme athlete Ash Dykes was paddling along the placid waters of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River flowing through Cameroon, Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo, when something stirred underneath his vessel, kicking up bubbles. Dykes, with the local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire and cameraman Will Perez, had just pushed off on a kayaking trip through the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike. The team knew they might encounter lowland gorillas, or perhaps forest elephants, as they made their way nearly 500 miles down the river. Perez then brought up another possible cause for the sudden ripples: a hippo. If the travelers had happened upon a hippopotamus, as many locals had warned them about, they were in immediate peril.

In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.

It has been revealed that when Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok. The thousands-deep comments section, full of viewers hooked as to what might happen next, burst with theories: Some swore that Mami Wata, a water spirit mentioned to frequent the riverbanks, had caused the sudden movement. One user mused that the three men were in “a real game of Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while others zoomed in on Perez’s visibly tense expression. Another user quipped: “I quit my job to focus on this expedition.”.

Sources indicate that though intended as a joke, the latter reaction succinctly illustrates the attention this trip has garnered on social media. For weeks millions of viewers were glued to the team’s frequent TikTok dispatches—which they later fleshed out into a longer YouTube series of deep dives. The videos documented the logistical hurdles in reaching the Sangha; their trudging amid the heat and threat of parasites and disease; their day spent with the Ba’Aka people, a seminomadic Indigenous tribe in Dzanga-Sangha Protected Area, where they foraged for wild coconut and joined a traditional hunt; and extended stretches of the three bobbing through calm waters. Those following online celebrated alongside the men when they spotted forest elephants, and their pulses quickened when they outran a swarm of bees chasing their kayaks. When the team went abruptly silent for a prolonged stretch, following a power bank failure, viewers worried that something catastrophic had happened.

The Congo Basin is the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike.

Sources indicate that the Sangha expedition—or “mission,” as Dykes has dubbed it—was the first leg in an ambitious undertaking called Project 6. The venture involves the Welshman—who’s made a career of adventure travel and breaking world records (such as becoming the first person to walk the length of the 4,000-mile-long Yangtze River, which took him nearly a year)—traverse “extreme” parts of the globe by performing intensive feats of athleticism. He will soon cross Kyrgyzstan on horseback in subzero temperatures for the second installment of the project; he is revealing ensuing stops one by one.

Sources indicate that “I'm fascinated with corners of the world that I am unfamiliar with and learning from the people there that call it home,” Dykes indicates. “Then [it’s] mixed in with the challenge of: Can I do what is deemed impossible, or can I do what people have tried to do before but failed to complete?”.

Aside from accomplishing the athletic challenge of constantly paddling down the Sangha every day for weeks, Dykes notes he aimed to showcase the beauty of the Congo Basin, and its inhabitants, in a responsible way—stressing to viewers that “you can go to places like this as long as you put the right preparation in,” he says.

Videos on TikTok and Youtube indicated the trio of Tuyumvire, Perez, and Dykes on their river adventure.

According to recent reports, dykes is quick to credit those who made the Congo Basin excursion possible—especially Tuyumvire, who works in conservation advocacy and ecotourism through his Kigali-based organization, Kumbukumbu Tours. Born in a forest village near Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, he fled the region following the civil war and lived in a refugee camp for over a decade before founding his tour company in 2015; he says those experiences shaped his belief that responsible tourism can be a means of helping make a local impact, particularly for young people. Tuyumvire agreed to join Dykes’s excursion because he saw an opportunity to tell meaningful stories about the Congo Basin for a larger audience.

In a recent development, “Because we have been surviving these out-of-context stories or even more exaggerated stories,” says Tuyumvire. “I myself feel the responsibility to always say yes to someone who has the microphone, and I tell the right context.”.

According to recent reports, ahead of the excursion Tuyumvire worked with Dykes to pick the specific location for the journey and scouted out the upper headwaters of the Sangha. Tuyumvire offered context and commentary in videos throughout the trip, speaking about the critical endangerment of forest elephants, the deforestation threatening the Congo Basin, and noting that women were on the front lines of hunting when they met the Ba’Aka people.

Yet straddling the line between education and entertainment for a predominantly TikTok viewership resulted in unexpected tensions. Internet connectivity posed a challenge due to the forest canopy; still, Dykes insisted the journey be “as live as possible” online. “I can’t be claiming that this is a lifetime expedition and then we use either recycled content or we go dark,” he notes.

Forest elephants are among the wildlife that inhabits the Congo Basin through which the team traveled.

While a plurality of viewers seemed genuinely fascinated by the three-week-long trip, even during less-exciting moments, Dykes noticed that some expressed a morbid glee for destructive content. Dykes states that some online commenters even started to bet money on how the trio might die in the Congo Basin, perhaps at the hands of a hippopotamus or a crocodile. “I think people are lost or confused as to what is a video game and what is a movie, and then what is reality,” he says. “So it's almost like this disconnect where people just wanted to be entertained: ‘If I'm going to the Congo, I want to see you escaping wildlife, wrestling.’” Tuyumvire saw the conflicting responses from viewers as “another kind of challenge for me to…create a story that will continuously be fed to the audience, but that will not also be overcrowded by too much exaggeration.”.

Recent findings suggest that others have criticized Dykes, drawing parallels between him and other foreigners entering so-called forbidding places and, intentionally or not, reinforcing outdated tropes. Guy Dieudonne Moukandi N'Kaya, a lecturer and researcher at Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, indicates that Dykes’s trip through the Sangha felt honest in that it showed the “tense coexistence” between humans and wildlife in the region. Yet the way Dykes framed the expedition gave N’Kaya pause: Leading up to the trip, Dykes noted in a TikTok teaser that he would be “dropping into the heart of darkness,” a phrase culled from Joseph Conrad’s controversial, turn-of-the-20th-century novella about a Belgian trading company siphoning resources from the Congo River. N’Kaya says that descriptors such as “heart of darkness” and “unexplored,” which Dykes has also used in some of his posts, erase the presence of those who have long lived within the region: “The Sangha is not empty,” N’Kaya writes over email. “For centuries it has been traversed by people in dug-out canoes—fisherfolk, traders, and families.”.

The water of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River, is tranquil—but the threat of disease-carrying bugs, dangerous wildlife, and the physical challenge of traveling 500 miles on human power made this one of Dykes' six missions.

According to recent reports, while Dykes emphasizes that he wanted to raise awareness of the Congo Basin, which is under dire threat of deforestation, some viewers have questioned whether the adventure has truly benefited the region—or whether it’s more of a boon to his Project 6 venture. The Congo Basin has long grappled with interlacing concerns including extreme poverty, corruption, and illegal mineral mining, which Tuyumvire says stem from the legacy of colonialism and slavery. “People are poor in the sense that they are ready to sell anything they are able to, to be able to just survive,” Tuyumvire says. “People seeing a white person in this region, it brings memories of the past: ‘This guy’s coming for timber. This guy’s coming for minerals.’ Things that really don't give them any kind of hope to develop the area. And that itself, the mindset, is a threat to the forest.”.

After returning from the trip in late October, Tuyumvire has been resting and resuming his routine following the physical demands of kayaking. He’d never kayaked at length before a few weeks ago; he says his real motivation was to “share the stories and to try to transform the adventure into something impactful.” The widespread interest in the videos hasn't translated to bookings of his tours, but that was never the goal: “The audience we had is not an audience of travelers, to be honest,” he says. He has been reflecting on how, in hindsight, he wishes he had created a stronger call to action so that TikTok viewers’ curiosity could have a direct impact on the region. (Alongside his tours Tuyumvire helps run the Congo Rainforest Fund, a local NGO that works with local communities to understand threats to the forest and create solutions, such as shoring up educational efforts and job opportunities.).

But he believes that broadcasting the journey did help viewers further understand a place that they may not have been familiar with. “[The] Congo Basin has been represented as a difficult place to access, a difficult, complex place to understand,” Tuyumvire indicates. “So people were saying, ‘Finally, someone is going to give us the real information’…we want to see them in the reality.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots.
  • In a recent development, in 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies.
  • In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In a recent development, in 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

Recent findings suggest that the whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic introduced in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

In a recent development, let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter manufacturer which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Recent findings suggest that travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

According to recent reports, the truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

Sources indicate that that’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

In a recent development, everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

It has been revealed that on real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

Industry observers note that the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

Sources indicate that all the great, major airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

In a recent development, tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and tech giant books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

In a recent development, I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his manufacturer ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

It has been revealed that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or newly introduced seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a latest golden age, again.

#30682. What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2341 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großarl Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.
  • It has been revealed that in Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state.
  • Großarl Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großarl Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.

It has been revealed that in Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate.

Großarl Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.

In a recent development, originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by massive name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany’s neighbor, Austria.

Language, of course, falls short when attempting to describe what Lebensgefühl means in practice; this complete awareness of being is a physicality, an emotion, a lifestyle, and a philosophy all rolled into one. It can’t be described, only felt (ah!). It’s the pleasure of simply existing. Leben (life), Gefühl (feeling). It’s an experience I wanted to understand firsthand. So when I found myself in Munich, less than a two-hour train ride from Hotel Nesslerhof, with a lifelong friend oblivious to my schemes, I decided it was time to get to the bottom of it.

Recent findings suggest that the root of Lebensgefühl is being entirely present in a moment: a conscious effort to slow down, gauge your own energy in the here and now, and choose the way you want to live your life accordingly. While the Austrian National Tourist Board uses the concept of Lebensgefühl as a marketing language, the feeling itself is real–and you can cultivate it anywhere. Admittedly, though—hand of accountability raised—it’s a whole lot easier when you’re surrounded by the postcard-perfect Austrian Alps.

Sources indicate that reaching this state of awareness requires an analog attention span and total presence. This is exactly what is demanded of you at Hotel Nesslerhof, which has dubbed itself the “natural happiness hotel.” The sprawling, sun-warmed property is an emerald-colored garden punctured by buttery blonde oak 1643 Austrian longhouse architecture. Here, the world is calm. Quiet.

Sources indicate that I arrive burned out, my attention scattered across screens and obligations. Stepping into a place fully immersed in nature with nothing expected of me, is jarring. It's been a while since I've consumed life this way. We’re conditioned to scroll, desire, save, project, and imagine, rather than to simply be—even to just be for a little bit.

Sources indicate that finding the answer started with carving out time and space, and letting go of everything I thought presence was supposed to look like. Next thing, I was naked in Austria with 40 strangers wondering the same thing.

Natural swimming pond for post-sauna plunges in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

Industry observers note that the hotel’s dedicated wellness area features five co-ed clothing-optional saunas (plus an additional private sauna in select suites), a salt steam bath, infrared loungers, and expansive natural swimming pools. To practice, or fully embody, Lebensgefühl successfully, you must be aware of your environment. At Nesslerhof, the alpine nature allows your body to break away from any externally imposed schedules and return back to your natural circadian rhythm, where an omniscient digital third person doesn't determine your flow; you do.

A Swiss pine sauna in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

According to recent reports, as a lifelong advocate for a good time, I mustered some gumption to join one of the daily themed sauna “infusions.” During these sessions, a sauna master leads thematic experiences using natural, regional botanicals like thyme, sage, Swiss stone pine, and eucalyptus. It’s held in the adults-only sauna event room, a space large enough to accommodate nearly 50 people.

It has been revealed that I walk in—towel on—and it occurs to me I’m the one making it weird here. There’s a lot I can swallow in life, but one thing I certainly will not do is be the person making things weird in a room. So, I lose the towel, join the crowd, and, in a state of mild panic, take a seat on the floor. Now, retrospectively speaking, I couldn’t grasp how all my choices in life had led me to this single, very conscious state of nudity in front of 40 Austrian strangers. There I was—sitting on the floor, completely floored. Which actually made things weirder, because I was later told you aren’t supposed to sit on the floor.

It has been revealed that enter the sauna master. Also nude. A sauna master is like a spiritual guide to a proper schvitz, and the infusions at Nesslerhof are next level material. At pivotal moments, I’m watching him execute rainbow ice acrobatics, teasing large, colorful chunks of ice around the room in a giant spoon before launching them onto the glowing-hot stones. Steam is sizzling everywhere as thick aromatics sweep across the room.

Hotel Nesslerhof's outdoor saltwater pool (with indoor access) surrounded by the Großarl Valley.

According to recent reports, and it’s hot. To make matters worse for myself—still on the floor—we’re given a natural body scrub to apply. So, whatever, sure: I start scrubbing amidst the rainbow ice, dense botanical air, and naked strangers unabashedly sprawled across the room in their entirety. I begin to gain consciousness of the palpable sense of self-assurance emanating from everyone as they laughed and chatted heart-to-heart. They were all having…fun. Slowly, decidedly, I reach a state of compos mentis: the only thing mortifying about this experience is my belief that this is a mortifying experience. This is not an intimidating reality. In fact, it’s pretty funny—and wildly inclusive, despite the fact that no one here speaks English but me. For the first time since arriving here, I feel entirely in the moment, free from any pressure to make it something else. I’m there, existing. I watch as my friend walks by the glass door and we lock eyes—him sending a distress call, and me, now a part of the sauna hijinks, completely in on the bit. Yeah, we’re all naked. So what?

Over the next three days, I continue this conversation with myself about the humility of physical form, alternating between stone pine saunas and crystal-clear mountain ponds. One amber afternoon, as I float between lily pads dotted by flowers and busy dragonflies, I stare at the burgeoning purple-pink Austrian Alps blanketing me, and I remember what it’s like to feel small again. Perception, both of ourselves and from others, has never really been that serious, has it? This is the body that’s given me life, the body that makes everything I do possible. Suddenly, I’m aware of every inch, from my fingertips to my toes. And I’m aware of my awareness. Lebensgefühl, for sure.

It has been revealed that mid-mind-body connection, a group of Austrian regulars hand-signals for me to come over for a beer. “For the electrolytes” is their roundabout scientific mojo after two to three courses of saunas and plunges. I catch what feels like an illegal glimpse of myself in the reflection of a sauna door and laugh. Gratitude emerges.

Hotel Nesslerhof's 800 m² natural swimming pond surrounded by a sunbathing lawn.

Industry observers note that gratitude for your body means food is more than just fuel, it’s an offering. The art of a meal has been a ritualistic practice since we were homo erectus: slowing down to practicing eating as an experience, not a function. And an eating environment can communicate a lot: savor this, stay with me, I’m here.

At Nesslerhof, eating was a slow and meditative practice, always beginning with a dedicated space: a seat at their table that was mine for my entire visit, an altar of sorts. Libations aplenty. In Austria, the Vorspeisensuppe—the traditional first-course soup—is served before almost every meal as a ceremonial anchor of hospitality and warmth. It’s often a non-negotiable, and acts as a symbolic moment to ground yourself before eating, or, as I’m practicing as an honorary Austrian here, to ground myself in a state of Lebensgefühl. For breakfast, lunch, dinner, and even the occasional snack, the soup is served first, and my brain instantly locks into being entirely in the moment. How could I not—I’m sipping on fresh ginger, carrot, and seasonal herb soups pulled directly from the mountains of Großarl—the lush valley an hour outside of Salzburg where the property sits.

Daily breakfast spread by the “Gästeflüsterer” team, including a wide selection of regional specialties.

Austrian Zwiebelrostbraten (pan-seared beef roast with crispy fried onions) served with seasonal Alpine accompaniments from the Großarl Valley.

When you are sick, what do you feed yourself to get better? How do people care for you using food? A lot of roads lead back to soup. It’s nourishing, easy for a strained body to digest, and a slow, intentional practice. It’s an antidote to hurriedness, a gateway to culinary Lebensgefühl.

Outside of the soup, a daily breakfast and lunch menu of fresh regional dishes, served on a strict schedule in the main parlor, makes indecision obsolete. In the evening, a five-course dinner at Atelier N, the hotel’s dedicated dining space, feels like stepping into an Austrian grandmother’s kitchen and hitting all the classics: Perftillbauer lamb, roast venison, fried veal Butterschnitzel, and pan-fried fish fillets. Everything is local, organic, and rooted in a genuine "nose-to-tail" principle—completely free of pretentious trends. And everyone here is known by their first name. The baker, Toni, brings fresh bread and pastries every morning. Elisabeth crafts the butter, curd cheese, yogurt, and whey—a real lactose lady. Anni and Sepp Inhög’s bees live on the sunniest side of the valley, which means their honey is something else entirely. Fresh local salmon trout, rainbow trout, brook trout, Arctic char, and local game are sourced directly from the nearby Hohe Tauern National Park. It’s a literal "alp-to-table" dining experience.

Kreuzkogel mountain in the Großarl Valley, accessed by the Kieserlbahn cable car.

The writer stopping for wild blueberries on a hike in the Austrian Alps.

It has been revealed that hotel Nesslerhof's hospitality was the last dance to Lebensgefühl. Longing for an escape–more often than not–coincides with a longing to feel in touch with yourself again. A weltanschauung, or worldview, can easily become skewed by the monotony of everyday life, which is why it takes displacement to course-correct. Human connection—which in this case took the form of the warm hospitality of Nesslerhof's staff—can serve as the intermediary. An agent [what do you that can create safe third spaces, and abstractly direct you to where your values lie.

On a hike just outside Nesslerhof’s front door in Hohe Tauern National Park, I meet one of Hotel Nesslerhof’s owners, Tina Neudegger. She built the property from the ground up with her husband, Hermann, and their three daughters. That’s over 40 years of family tradition and expertise coursing through this space. Tina is a consumingly luminous person, a natural caregiver. What she fosters at the property extends beyond hospitality–it’s a sense of security. It’s a maternal, comforting awareness that I am entirely taken care of, that my environment is safe, and that I don’t need to be on the defense. At Nesslerhof, I receive the same attention she gives her daughters and her husband, who treat the hotel like their home because, well, it is their home.

Employing my primate purpose, step by step with Tina as I teeter along an intimidating alpine cliffside, and attempting to eat a handful of fresh berries I covertly hoarded from a wily bush because I couldn't stop myself, I tune into her flow. We talk about how life can be a comedy of errors, and how we as humans cling to a gravitas that seems funny from a higher perspective. “Life’s simple. You can do anything once, right? So do it,” is Tina’s cheeky motto, something that makes all the seriousness in the world abruptly fade. I’m arrested by the smell of cows and am drawn back to the present. Weirdly, I like it.

The writer above Großarl Valley with Austrian libation.

The August 2026 total solar eclipse dips behind the Austrian Alps.

In a recent development, later, Tina drives me up the mountain to watch the solar eclipse from Wolke7, her family’s ski lodge, which is normally reached by the Kieserlbahn cable car adjacent to the hotel. We’re on a 40-minute, long, winding road up the Austrian Alps that feels alarmingly close to vertical. I’m bearing intense witness to the fact that there’s no guardrail, but I'm at ease knowing I can free my gaze because of Tina's confidence. We continue on a path that’s already there, a path that's always been there, a path that will always be there. Something about that feels nice. At the summit, I meet the family she’s created in Großarl: her eclectic collection of friends who uphold this alpine town's legacy. They look at her with complete adoration as they pass me homemade Kaiserschmarrn and a Radler. We watch the eclipse slowly fade behind the Austrian Alps—the totality of it lasting just over two minutes.

Sources indicate that but as I stand there, witnessing the world in its most sublime form, surrounded by Tina’s friends, who are vivid, complex, and completely magnanimous, the awe I feel expands from my chest, and those two minutes feel endless. I dub Tina the Mayor of Großarl, and as I overlook her valley, 6,500 meters above sea level, I see the whole picture again. At its deepest level, Lebensgefühl–your Lebensphilosophie–is painfully simple. What made you feel alive today? Build the environment for it. Pause and marvel. Continue forward.

Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.
  • But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.
  • The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., mentioned the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

It has been revealed that “I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

According to recent reports, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators remarked. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Sources indicate that hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer noted.

In a recent development, john M. Donnelly contributed to the report.
