Recent findings suggest that this past summer, my girlfriends and I packed our bags and headed to Rosemary Beach, Florida, for a bachelorette trip. Thirty minutes before landing, we collectively decided it was time for a quick refresh on the plane, pulling off our under-eye patches, applying lip liner, and attempting to tack on a little bit of makeup. I opened up my iPhone camera to guide me, but I could barely see what I was doing since the plane lights were off. You can imagine my surprise—and envy—when my best friend, Deanna, illuminated our row with her travel makeup mirror. It seemingly came out nowhere, and was already propped up on her seat tray, showing her exactly where she needed a touch-up. “I'm gonna need to borrow that,” I noted.

The pre-flight touch-up was not the only time Deanna's travel makeup mirror came in handy on our trip. One night before dinner, as 12 girls simultaneously got ready, she and I realized we were running short on bathroom mirrors. Rather than wait for the bathroom to clear and be forced to rush, or be late, we took turns doing our makeup with her travel mirror. Before we landed back at Newark Airport after the trip, I had already ordered Funtouch's travel makeup mirror for myself on Amazon.

Commerce editor Meaghan Kenny is using the Funtouch travel makeup mirror in the car.

Industry observers note that after a few months of having my own, I can honestly say this $17 travel accessory is worth every penny. While I initially envisioned using it on the plane or a crowded girls trip, it's proven handy on numerous occasions. Most recently, on a trip to Newport, Rhode Island, I pulled out my foldable travel mirror and did my makeup en-route. It was a relief to arrive at The Vanderbilt hotel looking and feeling put together, without having to sit through the whole four-hour car ride with a full face of makeup on first thing in the morning.

It's very simple to use: Unfold the mirror to reveal its full size, then tap the touch-screen button in the center to turn on the light. It offers three different light settings, including white light (my favorite), warm light, and cool light. The same button turns the light off too. And if that's a little too much light, say on an early morning flight, you can long press the touch-screen button to dim the brightness level. Another perk: The mirror stands up on its own, so you don't have to worry about holding it or propping it up against anything.

The travel makeup mirror has three different light settings to choose from.

Sources indicate that I love that the device is wireless. It comes with a USB charger so I can make sure it's powered up before I travel with it and leave the cord at home. The battery life is pretty impressive—I didn't need to recharge it after my four-day trip to Rhode Island. The portable device is also very slim—about the size of a Kindle or an iPad Mini—so it can be slipped into a tote bag, backpack, or weekender bag with ease. Its exterior is pretty durable too, so I don't need to worry about it getting crushed in my bag.

Sources indicate that another thing I appreciate about this travel makeup mirror: no magnification—I don't need to see my pores that close! The mirror is just the right size to show you your full face, head, and neck without being bulky or heavy to travel with. It's lightweight, compact, and portable—the trifecta of any good travel accessory. If you're stumped on what to get someone you love this season, surprise them with something they'll actually use every time they travel. You might want to grab one for yourself too.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, a friend gifted me this two-sided compact mirror from Chanel. Not only is it super sleek, but it's small enough to fit in my tiniest purses. I never leave the house for a date night or girls dinner without it. It's the perfect size for me to swiftly pull out to touch up my lip liner in an Uber or at a restaurant. It's a practical yet glamorous stocking stuffer for the friend who's always on the go.

This Amazon find earns major points for its versatility. The foldable mirror with LED lights can be rotated, and its stand can be adjusted to different heights. There's also a spot at the base of the mirror's stand that can hold your phone, so you can follow a makeup tutorial or watch a movie while you get ready.

Recent findings suggest that this travel makeup mirror looks pretty similar to mine, but it has a few extra bells and whistles. For starters, it features a adjustable stand that can be rotated back and forth to give you the best angle. It also has a smart sensing system, meaning the mirror lights up automatically when you open it, and turns off when the device is closed. If you, unlike me, do enjoy seeing your pores up close, this option comes with a small, detachable magnifying mirror.

It has been revealed that another foldable travel mirror, this one features a row of LED lights and a touch-screen button that can be used to adjust the brightness level. This compact mirror is smaller than iPhone, making it a smart choice for smaller bags or those just in case moments.

It has been revealed that smaller than a credit card and cheaper than an iced coffee, this $4 compact mirror is just the right size to slip into a purse or crossbody bag. Consider it your secret weapon to check if you have anything stuck in your teeth after dinner, or if you need another swipe of lipstick. No one will be the wiser!

The Best Places to Go in North America and the Caribbean in 2027

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that how we choose where to travel next can vary greatly.
  • Industry observers note that consider Jamaica’s South Coast: In the wake of Hurricane Melissa, you can support communities leading their own recovery, and still enjoy the turquoise waters, farm-to-table dinners, and design-forward boutique stays as rewards along the way.
  • Recent findings suggest that then there are the places revealing new dimensions beyond what first put them on the map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that how we choose where to travel next can vary greatly. Sometimes it’s a long-held fantasy, originally spurred by a book or a movie; other times, a trusted recommendation from a discerning friend. Increasingly, it’s a single image encountered online—the curve of a sandy cove, the tangled streets of a medieval old town, or a terrace set aglow at golden hour—that prompts us to hit Save. Our annual list of the best places to go takes a more considered approach, pairing the where with the why now. When it comes to the best places to go in North America—a confoundingly diverse set of landscapes that spans 9.5 million square miles—that motivation feels especially relevant: a recognition that the way we travel matters as much as where we go.

Industry observers note that consider Jamaica’s South Coast: In the wake of Hurricane Melissa, you can support communities leading their own recovery, and still enjoy the turquoise waters, farm-to-table dinners, and design-forward boutique stays as rewards along the way. Meanwhile, tiny and culturally rich Curaçao is riding a wave of attention as a FIFA World Cup darling, and fresh flights and resorts showcase the island’s equally enticing on-the-ground energy. In Canada’s British Columbia, Clayoquot remains a secluded sweep of pristine wilderness. Here a new floating lodge owned by the Ahousaht First Nation is creating novel ways to experience this extraordinary landscape while engaging more deeply with its culture: Walk beneath ancient cedars. Soak in geothermal pools. Listen, learn, and slow down.

Recent findings suggest that then there are the places revealing new dimensions beyond what first put them on the map. Oregon’s Willamette Valley, beloved by Pinot Noir devotees, is melding a varied and sophisticated food scene with its farm-first, sustainability-minded ethos. In Taos, New Mexico, an arts and cultural renaissance is unfolding against a backdrop of high-altitude adventure, and standout new restaurants will make sure you’re well-fueled for all the wandering.

Each destination on this list comes with expert-backed picks for where to stay, what to eat, and what to do, so you can start planning every aspect of your trip immediately. Follow us into 2027 as we continue to share more about these journeys with on-the-ground reporting and enough inspiration to fill your calendar. See you on the road! —Arati Menon.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: wild coastal landscapes and a groundbreaking new Indigenous-owned luxury lodge.

The land and waters of UNESCO-designated biosphere Clayoquot Sound have been stewarded by the First Nations for generations.

Kayaking, whale-watching, and hiking excursions can be coordinated directly through the lodges.

Clayoquot Sound has long drawn adventurous travelers to Vancouver Island’s wild western edge—a maze of forested islands, secluded inlets, and old-growth rainforests. But now, Indigenous-owned hospitality is giving this remote luxury escape a deeper sense of place, shaped by the First Nations that have stewarded its lands and waters for generations.

A UNESCO-designated biosphere region spanning nearly 864,868 acres of land and sea, Clayoquot Sound is already home to the much-lauded Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge. But the July 2026 opening of Wahous Wilderness Lodge in secluded Quait Bay introduces a different kind of high-end stay. Owned and operated by the Ahousaht First Nation, the 16-room floating lodge and four forest cabins were reacquired in 2022 by the Nation’s hereditary chiefs through the Maaqutusiis Hahoulthee Stewardship Society (MHSS). Guests are welcomed into Ahousaht territory with tide-to-table dining, a shoreline spa, and a ceremonial welcome in the cedar longhouse. A stay begins and ends in the longhouse, concluding with a traditional klup-chus-tapčas, or salmon barbecue, in an evening that brings together food, storytelling, and cultural exchange in a final gathering rooted in Ahousaht tradition.

According to recent reports, the three-Michelin-key Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge is evolving too. Set on 600 acres at the mouth of the Bedwell River, the off-grid retreat is known for its 25 safari-style canvas tents, cedar-plank boardwalks, and wilderness adventures. Newer experiences in 2026 include after-dark bioluminescence kayaking, a floating sauna, and a guided walk across Flores Island through Ahousaht territory.

Fresh experiences and places to stay aside, Clayoquot Sound remains remote enough to preserve its deep sense of seclusion. This vast coastal labyrinth is best explored by water and on foot: Paddle between forested islands, walk beneath ancient cedars on Meares Island, hike Flores Island’s remote Wildside Trail, or soak in the geothermal pools at Hot Springs Cove. From March to October, join a whale-watching trip to spot orcas, humpbacks, or grey whales. Elsewhere, wildlife may simply find you: Black bears forage along the shoreline at low tide, and sea otters paddle through the inlets. Some excursions can be arranged directly through the lodges, while Tofino-based operators, such as Ahousaht-owned Ahous Adventures or Tofino Water Taxi, make the wider sound accessible. —Ashleigh Stewart.

Go for: an island culture bursting with color, rhythm, and Blue Wave energy.

Curaçao’s UNESCO-listed capital, Willemstad, is a vibrant blend of European, African, and Caribbean influences.

New nonstop flights from major US airports include American Airlines’ seasonal Chicago O’Hare route from December to April.

According to recent reports, in 2026 the tiny Caribbean island of Curaçao made history as the least-populated nation to ever compete in the FIFA World Cup and stole hearts along the way. But the exuberant “Blue Wave” was just a taste of the vibrant energy humming across this 171-square-mile Dutch Caribbean island. In Willemstad, the UNESCO-listed capital, Curaçao’s multicultural spirit—rooted in European, African, and Caribbean influences—is on vivid display. Pastel Dutch colonial buildings house eclectic pubs, boutique galleries, and jazz cafés reverberating with tumba, a blend of Afro-Caribbean and Latin jazz.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of 2026, Curaçao will welcome two newly introduced resorts that promise buzzy stays with access to all of the above. The adults-only, 305-key Pyrmont Curaçao, an Autograph Collection All-Inclusive Resort will occupy a beachfront stretch in Willemstad’s bohemian Pietermaai neighborhood, a walkable historic district with a side of nightlife. Here, they will reimagine one 19th-century Neoclassical mansion as a spa, and another as one of six restaurants and bars. In the quieter northwest, which is home to some of the island’s most scenic beaches and national parks, the 297-room Tui Blue Curaçao will feature swim-up suites, six Caribbean restaurants, and a private beach on aquamarine Santa Martha Bay, with daily yoga sessions on the sand. In more good news, the island is also easier to reach than ever before: New nonstop flights from major US airports include American Airlines’ seasonal route that runs from December through April from Chicago O’Hare, rolled out in late 2025. —Jessica Puckett.

Go for: an off-the-beaten-path, community-focused escape—and a chance to support tourism’s recovery after Hurricane Melissa.

South Coast's Treasure Beach has become known for its boutique properties such as Jakes Hotel, founded by local artist Sally Henzell.

Sources indicate that this October marks the one-year anniversary of Hurricane Melissa, the strongest and costliest hurricane to ever hit Jamaica. With most of the damage centered in the west and southwest of the island, Jamaica’s South Coast has been at the forefront of recovery efforts—and is now welcoming travelers back with open arms.

According to recent reports, jamaica is so much more than reggae and resorts, and there’s never been a better time for more meaningful travel to one of its most under-the-radar coastal regions. The best-known South Coast area, Treasure Beach, is a mellow seaside town known for its black sand beaches and slow-paced bohemian lifestyle. Every other year, it’s also host to the Calabash International Literary Festival, the largest in the Caribbean (in 2027 it will be held in May). The beaches here are lined with colorful guesthouses and design-forward boutique stays like Jakes Hotel, a beloved family-run establishment founded by local artist Sally Henzell. Further up the coast, Bluefields Bay Villas & Suites is another family-run gem that reopened in February 2026. For a resort stay, Sandals South Coast will reopen in November 2026 following a multimillion-dollar renovation.

It’s also become easier for travelers to pair the beachy South Coast with the lush hills of St. Elizabeth Parish—Jamaica’s breadbasket. The island’s agriculture industry took the biggest hit from the hurricane, prompting Jakes Hotel to double down on its agro-tourism offerings. In March, the hotel released farm tours and monthly full-moon farm-to-table dinners for guests; its nonprofit arm also provides direct cash grants and equipment vouchers to farmers in the region.

Recent findings suggest that for travelers planning a longer trip, the drive between Negril and Treasure Beach is one of Jamaica’s most scenic. Along the way, stop at the natural swimming pools at YS Falls, sample Jamaican street food beneath the shaded archway of Bamboo Avenue (don’t skip Middle Quarters’ famous peppered shrimp), and take a dip in the turquoise waters of Bluefields Bay. If you have a few days to spare, continue driving east to Kingston, the urban epicenter of Jamaican nightlife and culture. —Hannah Towey.

Go for: Tennessee’s other music city whose evolving arts scene is going massive.

The riverfront Memphis Flyway, an elevated walkway in Tom Lee Park, opened June 2026.

The walkway has become an ideal spot for bird-watchers that intersects with several major migratory routes.

The city of Memphis is best known as a cradle for all things low and slow, from the city’s signature hickory-smoked ribs to the moody numbers emanating from the blues clubs on Beale Street. But the west Tennessean cultural icon also knows how to pick up the tempo, and in 2027 its revitalized arts scene will be in full swing.

As the state’s largest majority-Black city, Memphis is showing off its rich cultural tapestry with the back-and-better-than-ever Memphis Art Museum—the state’s oldest and largest. Facilities reopen in December 2026 at a reimagined three-acre campus located downtown. The new legroom includes a 10,000-square-foot courtyard and a sprawling rooftop sculpture garden. But the real pièce de résistance is what’s on the inside: Inaugural exhibitions revisit and subvert history, from “Rhapsodies in Black,” an examination of the interplay between jazz and Black American abstraction, to “Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984,” a look back on Hook Brothers, a legendary photography studio that documented Black life in Memphis from 1907 until 1979.

Sources indicate that long-anticipated renovations to the National Civil Rights Museum—including five interactive galleries dedicated to addressing the structural problems of poverty, education, housing, gender equality, and nonviolence—debuted earlier this May. The Metal Museum, one of the few institutions in the world dedicated to the craft, also celebrated a grand reopening in September.

For a breath of fresh air, the riverfront Memphis Flyway, an elevated walkway in Tom Lee Park, opened this June—an ideal spot for bird-watchers that intersects with several major migratory routes. Evenings are well spent at the newest venues in Tennessee’s second music city, like the 4,500-seat Grind City Amp, which opened in April 2026, followed by the intimate vinyl room at Satellite Music Hall in September.

It has been revealed that memphis’s food and hotel scenes also bring high notes to back it all up. Michelin’s inaugural American South edition honored five of the city’s restaurants, including farm-to-table Italian restaurant Hog & Hominy, which nabbed a Bib Gourmand. And when it comes to hospitality, in 2027 Memphis is in with the new thanks to projects like Cooper Hotel, an art-filled boutique set to join the thriving midtown Arts District. —Kat Chen.

Go for: a mountain road trip through Latest England’s wild side.

The White Mountains region comprises of nearly 800,000 acres including White Mountain National Forest, which stretches across central and northern Fresh Hampshire and slightly into western Maine.

If you want a New England trip where the scenery does all the talking, look to New Hampshire. The Granite State has long played second fiddle to its more famous neighbors, but that’s part of its appeal: Dense with forests, winding mountain roads, glassy lakes, and small towns, it’s wilder than coastal New England, less manicured than Vermont’s resort towns, and gloriously road-trip friendly. At its heart is the White Mountains, a roughly 800,000-acre region of high peaks, and White Mountain National Forest, which stretches across central and northern New Hampshire and slightly into western Maine.

It has been revealed that the region is getting harder to overlook, not least of all because lodgings are getting much more attractive. Under Canvas White Mountains opened on 86 acres in the quaint river town of Dalton in June 2026 with 45 safari-style tents, including stargazer tents with cutouts for gazing up at the night sky. In the scenic Monadnock region, The Inn at Hancock, New Hampshire’s oldest continuously operating inn, has reopened after a three-year restoration with 15 individually designed suites. In Bretton Woods, with grand-hotel history and significant mountain views, the iconic Omni Mount Washington Resort completed its major reimagining of its historic rooms and dining in July 2026.

Industry observers note that and the food scene has its own unique momentum: Born-and-bred Dover chef Evan Hennessey of Stages became New Hampshire’s first winner of the James Beard Best Chef: Northeast honor in 2026; his newer Topolino brings his Mediterranean-inspired dishes to a more casual setting. Make the trip to Seven Birches Winery in Lincoln for European-style classics and New England ciders enjoyed on a vineyard; it’s located within the recently renovated Riverwalk Resort, tucked away on sprawling Loon Mountain. Add a stately stay at seaside Portsmouth’s new Treadwell Mansion, in a Federal-style brick home, and you have a circuit that makes the Granite State feel both classic and freshly worth discovering. —Jessica Chapel.

Go for: world-class wine and a meteorically rising culinary scene with small-town vibes.

Restaurants such as Michelin-starred Alea Bakery and Cafe have cemented Willamette Valley's farm-first culinary scene.

South of Portland, Willamette Valley is Oregon's premier wine region—but also a mecca for truffle foraging and coastal pursuits.

Just south of Portland, Oregon’s premier wine region has attracted Pinot Noir devotees since 1985, when the valley’s signature grape beat French Burgundies in a blind tasting and stunned the world. Now winemakers are also earning international acclaim for Chardonnay and dialing in highly regarded traditional-method sparkling wine.

McMinnville is also adding refined lodging to the mix. Piquette, a 17-room boutique hotel, is slated to open on vibrant Alpine Avenue in early 2027. Following will be Marriott’s AC Retreat at Evergreen, which will offer vineyard views, a pool, and a wine bar. In Carlton, Shaughnessy’s team opened Lucky Duck, a two-bedroom rental in the small town’s original bank complete with a Hayward-stocked fridge. The result is an increasingly ambitious and food-focused wine destination that remains refreshingly unpretentious. —Rebecca Toy.

Go for: a vibrant culinary scene that puts fresh spins on familiar flavors in a long-loved beach city.

Beyond its beaches and robust surf culture, San Diego's restaurants—fresh and old—are redefining its culinary identity.

Sunny San Diego’s beautiful blue-water beaches have long lured laid-back surfers, while its world-class zoo has created generations of conservation-minded kids. But only recently has America’s Finest City emerged as a culinary mecca where savvy food lovers come in search of their next great meal.

Sources indicate that in the seaside community of La Jolla, long home to some of the county’s foundational restaurants, seasoned local chefs and a upcoming guard are making their mark. Consider native chef Travis Swikard of the lauded Cal-Med restaurant Callie, known for dishes like juicy Aleppo chicken and smoky harissa-grilled lamb chops. His sophomore spot, Fleurette, opened at the end of 2025 with a modern French Provençal cuisine that’s built around California ingredients—think Dover sole meunière amandine and buttery soft scrambled duck eggs with San Diego uni. Nearby at Michelin-starred Lucien, in the heart of downtown, a fresh cohort of Per Se alums crafts an intricate tasting menu that celebrates local farms and fishermen. A 20-minute drive north, in Carmel Valley, chef William Bradley’s recently redesigned Addison offers a contemporary Cali tasting menu. The three-Michelin-starred destination, housed in the Fairmont Grand Del Mar, just celebrated its 20th anniversary with the launch of a new champagne lounge—so slip in for a glass before dinner. If fast-fine dining is more your vibe, head to Encinitas, where Chick & Hawk serves spicy fried chicken sandwiches and craft cocktails in a space that pays homage to Southern California’s skate and surf culture of the ’80s and ’90s—which is fitting, given that skateboarding legend Tony Hawk is a partner. For a more intimate, upscale affair, head about 15 minutes up the 101 to idyllic Carlsbad, where the 22-seater Lilo serves a seafood-heavy tasting menu from chef Eric Bost, an LA transplant who has helped shape the city’s dining scene. But it’s not just the flashy new spots that make San Diego’s dining scene great. Barrio Logan’s legendary Las Cuatro Milpas relocated a few blocks away earlier in 2026 after nearly a century in business. While we miss the OG location, we’re happy to report the flour tortillas are still worth the journey.

In a recent development, you’ll need somewhere to rest between all those meals. In Coronado, the historic Hotel del Coronado unveiled a $550 million restoration in the summer of 2025, while the 31-room Baby Grand is its flashy maximalist foil. And over in Carlsbad the chic new Hotel Solea, Autograph Collection is within walking distance of Legoland. If that’s your draw, know that United Airlines started operating out of its local airport earlier this year. —Omar Mamoon.

Go for: pristine blue water, mountains, and a latest wave of boutique hotels and world-class restaurants.

Despite being a long-beloved weekend getaway in Canada, Simcoe County has flown under the radar for those outside the province seeking a culinary coastal getaway outside of ski season.

Newly introduced to North America’s 50 Best list, The Pine's husband-and-wife team put a spin on fine dining with dishes like a Shanghai-style lamb schnitzel served with a black-garlic-infused eggplant purée.

In a recent development, canada will always be associated with natural beauty: the Rocky Mountains of the west, the rugged coastline of the Maritimes, and the otherworldly fjords of Newfoundland. Only recently have people started looking closer to the middle of the country for their dose of outdoor adventure. Ontario, specifically the Simcoe and Grey County regions just a couple of hours northwest of Toronto, has long been a beloved weekend getaway for city folk—but has flown under the radar for those outside the province.

In a recent development, until recently, you most likely ended up here for a ski trip at Blue Mountain resort or as a guest at a friend’s cottage, as there was little in the way of notable accommodation. But upcoming hotels have popped up in the last few years: starting with the understatedly luxe The Dorchester hotel in 2022, followed by the hip and modern Somewhere Inn Collingwood in 2024, and, most recently, in July 2026, the nine-room Leeward House in the historic town of Thornbury.

The region is anchored by the beauty of Georgian Bay’s Caribbean-like waters and its rugged cliffs—a great place for swimming, boating, and caving in the summer, and complementing Blue Mountain’s Stay and Ski lodging-and-lift-ticket packages in the winter. However, if outdoor adventure isn’t your thing and your palate tends to dictate the itinerary, it has plenty to tempt, with a growing community of globally trained chefs bringing fresh energy to the local dining scene, while championing the producers and purveyors who define the region. Nowhere is this more evident than at The Pine, recently added to North America’s 50 Best list, where husband-and-wife team Jeremy and Cassie Austin are putting their spin on fine dining with a Chinese twist—expect dishes like a Shanghai-style lamb schnitzel served with a black-garlic-infused eggplant purée. They also opened seafood-focused Lore this June, where the menu features gussied-up tuna melts and playful, utterly delicious scallop nuggets. A scenic, 45-minute drive inland takes you to Down Home, where a weekly tasting menu places emphasis on produce from regenerative organic farms. There are plenty of casual but equally delicious options too, like Heart’s Tavern, where chef Teo Paul and partner Luke Wood bring a French bistro sensibility to a 19th-century farmhouse. Even the natural wine scene has found its way here with Chin Chin, a bar from which locals and visitors spill out onto sidewalk benches with glasses of wine and grazing boards stacked with freshly baked baguette and cheese. —Kyle Beechey.

Go for: a mountain town meets cultural hotbed.

Taos sits at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo mountains, part of the Newly introduced Mexico stretch of the Rockies.

In a recent development, boutique ski resorts famed for deep powder, narrow chutes, and a roster of high-altitude summer thrills. A thousand years of Indigenous arts and culture in one of the West's longest continuously inhabited pueblos. A buzzy contemporary art scene encompassing visual arts, film, music, installation, and craft. These all combine to create a magnetism that has drawn visitors to Taos ever since a ragtag group of creatives descended on the scrappy mountain town to found the Taos Society of Artists in 1915.

Sources indicate that the town’s pull is only getting stronger with a series of high-profile openings and reimaginations, from the unveiling of the spiffed-up historic Taos Plaza—its cultural and geographic center—this past summer to the anticipated fall 2027 opening of an ambitious Tribal Heritage Center. Occupying a 14-acre grant returning ancestral lands to the Taos Pueblo, the complex will feature a cultural center, restaurants, galleries, and a pueblo-inspired Marriott TownePlace Suites and Fairfield Inn & Suites. Also next year, the community observatory Cielo Centro, which will house the largest publicly accessible telescope in New Mexico, begins its phased opening with a 1,600-square-foot classroom building, an outdoor amphitheater, and an observation plaza. Recently, too, Hotel Willa, a 52-room motor lodge at the gateway to the Taos Arts District, has been retrofit as adobe-desert chic down to its sun-splashed pool, stargazing deck, gallery, and onsite art programming courtesy of the Paseo Project. Guests can shuttle to nearby ski areas in the hotel’s new electric Volkswagen ID.Buzz.

The best way to appreciate Taos’s role as a base camp for the surrounding Sangre de Cristo mountains is to drive the 84-mile Enchanted Circle Scenic Byway, or head straight for Taos Ski Valley, which debuted a upcoming, modern triple-chairlift last year as part of a multimillion-dollar renovation. Family-friendly resort Angel Fire, which offers snow tubing and the only night-skiing in the state, has vastly expanded access with the high-capacity Angel Express lift, whisking up to 1,800 riders an hour at a speed of 1,000 feet per minute. This upcoming year will see the return of the beloved outdoor Paseo Festival, known for envelope-pushing installations and performance art, which took a pause in 2026 to reboot as a biennial event. The Taos Film Festival, which debuted in 2026, returns April 29 to May 2 at the Taos Center for the Arts.

In a recent development, the little town punches above its culinary weight, too. Make sure to check out the newly opened Dawn Butterfly, the first modern, full-service restaurant inside Taos Pueblo, where local Carpio J. Bernal Jr. serves up indigenous heritage dishes like slow-roasted bison and blue cornmeal with chokecherry sauce. Suchness specializes in unexpected juxtapositions like lamb loin with Moroccan tomato jam and smoked eggplant and rigatoni topped with a smoked carrot Bolognese and vegan ricotta. And for breakfast sample the wood-fired bialy-style bagels topped with wild-caught salmon at Tomorrow and Tomorrow, or indulge in brunch at Juliette in Hotel Willa, where the Dutch pancake is a standout. —Melanie Haiken.

Go for: a seafood-forward wine country getaway—with elevated upcoming wellness stays.

The weathered granite mountains and rugged terrain of Valle de Guadalupe have greeted a newly introduced wave of hospitality offerings such as Mira Earth Studios.

Recent findings suggest that when you come to a stop at the sole traffic light in Mexico’s Valle de Guadalupe, you can see weathered granite mountains and rugged, sun-drenched terrain unfold in every direction. This is the environment that nurtures Mexico’s premier wine region, which might still be young and pliable but produces the mineral Chenin Blanc, the historic misión, unconventional red blends, and the pitch-dark nebbiolo that have drawn savvy oenophiles for years. The region’s culinary offerings are just as compelling: When the Michelin Guide México debuted in 2024, the state of Baja California, anchored by Valle de Guadalupe, emerged as the second-most-decorated region behind Mexico City. All of this awaits less than an hour by car from the closest US–Mexico border crossing point—and it is aging like fine wine.

Industry observers note that the 2026 edition of Mexico’s Michelin Guide spotlights several new restaurants, as well as esteemed ones. Damiana, which began as a pop-up and has since found a permanent home in the shade of trees at the Viñedos de la Reina winery, has energized the Valle with chef and co-owner Esteban Luis’s oceanic array of buttery spider crab croquettes, smoked Kumiai oysters, and bluefin tuna dressed with soy sauce then topped with gooseneck barnacle rings. Then there’s Olivea Farm to Table, led by chef Daniel Nates, which dazzles diners on an impressive farm tour that ends in the dining room, where plump mussels are steamed with saffron, and roasted aged duck is balanced by a pair of quenelles in an earthy blackberry sauce. Stalwarts like Animalón, a romantic campestre set under a 200-year-old live oak tree, and Lunario, in an intimate greenhouse-like building, have held on to their Michelin distinctions for innovative tasting menus—anchored in local seafood but also indigenous herbs and seasonal vegetables—that have helped define Baja California’s innovative cuisine.

A latest wave of hospitality offerings have quietly opened in recent years to meet this moment. And their flavor here is consistent: sustainable hotels committed to preserving viticulture. The amenity-rich Mira Earth Studios offers a curated selection of local wines, a hot tub, and an infrared sauna in each of its 10 studio suites, which are made of earth and tucked into the hillside. Hike up to the pool for a feast of raw shellfish served with a mosaic of sauces at Mira Fireside by chef José Luis Hinostroza. In like manner, the Banyan Tree Veya, built by renowned Mexican architect Michel Rojkind, features a private plunge pool and 30 villas, each with its own wide terrace, that recede into the landscape. Overlooking the property is Amapola, a showcase restaurant that serves the property’s Pictograma wines and regional ingredients like grilled spot prawns, callo catarina (scallops), and grilled quail over fideos in a minimalist style, courtesy of Baja California chefs Benito Molina and Solange Muris.

Industry observers note that there is more to come: Bruma Wine Estate—the hospitality juggernaut that houses iconic restaurants Fauna and Bruma Wine Garden, plus hotels Ático, Casa 8, and Casa Montaña—has a 62-room Montage Hotels and Resorts property targeted for 2028. Valle de Guadalupe has never been loud in its evolution, but with each passing year, it promises a richer experience. —Bill Esparza.

Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.
  • Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, mentioned legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.
  • “Yes, absolutely,” she noted when asked if the package would get a vote this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, mentioned legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she noted when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, stated she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses unveiled a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

It has been revealed that “Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had mentioned they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

In a recent development, the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack mentioned she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this glitch.”.

Recent findings suggest that leger Fernández noted if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández remarked. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a fresh strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was unveiled with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

Recent findings suggest that that’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

According to recent reports, I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO claims it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most crucial aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are significant business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the upcoming alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following….

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

According to recent reports, the food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

Recent findings suggest that in short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delta Air Lines and Hyatt have declared the much-anticipated details of their new loyalty partnership.

The newly introduced arrangement will allow certain SkyMiles and World of Hyatt members to “double dip” their earnings on flights and hotel stays.

That means you could earn both Delta miles and Hyatt points on a flight — or a hotel booking. The setup is reminiscent of what Hyatt previously shared with American Airlines.

However, there are two big rules to know about this Delta-Hyatt arrangement:.

For Delta Medallion and World of Hyatt elite members, this partnership will open up more ways to earn points and miles.

Plus, the partnership includes new loyalty perks that members can unlock as they climb the status ladder.

For instance, Delta will add Hyatt free-night certificates to its menu of choice benefits available at the Platinum and Diamond Medallion levels.

Hyatt elites can opt for Delta benefits like e-certificates and Sky Club passes as they reach certain milestones.

Let's get to the details of how to link your account, and how the earnings will work.

To start earning SkyMiles on Hyatt stays and World of Hyatt points on Delta flights, you’ll need to link your two loyalty accounts.

You can do that through this page on Delta’s website or this one via Hyatt’s.

You’ll start earning right away on eligible flights and hotel stays.

There are bonus points on the table for members who act promptly.

All members can earn those bonus points, whether they have elite status or not.

According to recent reports, even sooner, though, members who link their World of Hyatt and Delta SkyMiles accounts can register to earn one additional elite night credit on their first qualifying stay completed between Nov. 17 and Dec. 31, 2026. Eligible stays are those booked as paid or award nights.

Delta flyers who earn Medallion elite status will be eligible to earn SkyMiles on eligible Hyatt bookings.

Medallions will earn 1 mile per $1 of eligible spend at participating Hyatt properties.

You’ll earn those Delta miles on top of the standard points (and elite night credits) that you’d earn as a World of Hyatt member.

Similarly, World of Hyatt elite members can earn points on Delta flights.

That’s on top of the Delta miles (and Medallion Qualifying Dollars) you’d earn for your booking.

The rules here are a bit more nuanced:.

While Delta’s coach fares are not eligible for World of Hyatt earnings, you can still earn Hyatt points on the carrier’s basic premium fares like Comfort Basic, Basic business, etc.

This latest partnership between Delta SkyMiles and World of Hyatt certainly unlocks more earning opportunities for loyalty members across both programs.

The setup is clearly tilted heavily toward travelers who have status — and those who are willing to pay more for a premium ticket. You have to be “elite” to take full advantage of the tie-up, and can’t earn Hyatt points on a regular Delta main cabin booking.

However, travelers who are already committed Delta and Hyatt loyalists will come out ahead, gaining the ability to stack their earnings on both flights and hotel stays.

The SkyMiles-World of Hyatt partnership also includes a host of latest benefits that members of both programs can select as they earn higher status.

Those options will go live on Feb. 1, when Delta starts its new Medallion qualification year.

Before opting for a free night award, you'll obviously want to weigh that perk against the other options you have, which range from Sky Club memberships to travel vouchers on Delta.

Hyatt is also layering in Delta benefits to its menu of Milestone Rewards, which members can select upon hitting certain elite thresholds.

Beginning Jan. 1, World of Hyatt members will have new options to pick, including:.

This partnership is an exciting development for World of Hyatt and SkyMiles members. While most of the benefits will apply to those with elite status in the programs and those booking premium tickets on Delta. Still, for those travelers to whom this applies, this is a great fresh way to unlock additional rewards over the course of your annual travels.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Air travel in the U.S. was returning to normal Monday, even as the backlog from Friday’s massive air traffic control outage remained evident.

According to recent reports, flights across the country were taking off regularly, and the long lines seen at airports such as Atlanta and Latest York-JFK over the weekend were easing. Some travelers are still waiting on rescheduled flights, however, and there will likely be several hundred flight cancellations and thousands of delays as the day goes on.

Sources indicate that according to FlightAware, there were around 300 cancellations in the U.S. as of 9 a.m., which is already above average for an entire day of operations. There were about 1,270 delays.

Dallas/Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare, Charlotte, North Carolina, and Reagan National reported the highest number of cancellations and delays Monday morning.

It has been revealed that U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy remarked over the weekend that operations should be close to normal by Monday evening.

According to the DOT and FAA, the outage was caused by a router installed during an upgrade of ATC communications systems.

The contractor that performed that upgrade, Duffy mentioned Saturday, is L3Harris, a legacy technology provider for the FAA.

Either because of an installation mistake or a problem with the router itself, the router began “flooding” other routers in the system, the secretary stated, leading to the outage.

The FAA has not made a final determination about the cause, but in either case, “we’re going to hold people accountable,” Duffy said.

“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” he added. “A contractor didn’t meet the moment, or the equipment didn’t meet the moment.”.

Duffy also noted that L3Harris actually owns the ATC communications network.

“I can’t go somewhere else, they own it,” he remarked.

Clearly frustrated with the situation, Duffy broadened his criticism to other private companies performing work for the DOT.

It has been revealed that “Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us,” he mentioned. “Full stop. And we have demanded more.”.

“L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA,” the firm remarked in a statement released Saturday. “With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines, and air traffic operations seriously.”.

Industry observers note that the outage has also rekindled a months-long debate over funding for the DOT’s ongoing ATC modernization program. Duffy said Friday night that the FAA’s initial $30 billion target is no longer enough, and he now wants $50 billion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

According to recent reports, the race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

Industry observers note that the rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”.

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she remarked in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

It has been revealed that calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

It has been revealed that one incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#30673. Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3245 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania.
  • I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass.
  • The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania. Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away.

I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves.

The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.

Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats.

It has been revealed that it’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in.

Recent findings suggest that this is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle.

According to recent reports, by those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest.

Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel tech giant Zbulo, which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He notes the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the concern. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October.

According to recent reports, after breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol.

Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude.

According to recent reports, all except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain.

At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century.

Industry observers note that ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it.

It has been revealed that “This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.”.

According to recent reports, having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago, I know what he means. Besides the two of us and the eagle riding the thermals overhead, there isn’t another soul in sight.

Along the route, small guesthouses warmly welcome trekkers, who have created a reason to stay—or return—to communities once disrupted by conflict and emagration.

By late afternoon, after Van Dam and I part ways below Gjeravica. What appeared as a scattering of rooftops no bigger than a thumbnail now reveals itself in the distinct forms of summer homes and traditional katuns, seasonal shepherd settlements composed of simple huts and stone-walled livestock pens.

The family has only recently begun welcoming trekkers into their home, and they radiate the kind of excitement that comes from still being delighted by every single arrival. Renaja leads me to my room for the night, tucked on the third floor beneath the A-frame eaves. Downstairs, pizza bakes in an old wood-burning stove while Renaja's mother and grandmother set a long table for the dozen or so guests still dribbling in.

Sources indicate that the old highland idea of besa—that a house belongs not only to its owner, but to God and to the guest—is coming to life before my eyes. Or, as Fahrig, who first came to these mountains in 2012, later puts it: bukë, kripë, zemër, an Albanian expression meaning “bread, salt, and heart.” “The material offering may be simple,” he claims. “The welcome is what makes it memorable.”.

It has been revealed that the following morning, I continue deeper into Kosovo, eventually rejoining the main Peaks of the Balkans route. Now, it’s Montenegro on the other side of the invisible line I keep crossing. Over the coming days, the trail shifts between empty mountain passes and occasional stretches of asphalt—the latter one being a reason, Fahrig states, that many trekkers truncate this section entirely. He estimates that places such as the Rugova Gorge—a river-carved passage whose 2-3,000-foot-deep limestone walls bear stone-blasted tunnels, a frothy emerald river, and viewpoints at every turn—right now receive around 30 percent or less of the traffic funneled through Dobërdol.

The Peaks of the Balkans stitches together sections that include dirt paths, country roads, and sometimes asphalt—but even the less photogenic portions lead to impactful destinations.

In Drelaj, where this dramatic gorge opens into a wider pastoral valley, skipping Kosovo begins to feel like missing the point. This quiet highland hamlet is embraced on all sides by forested mountains. Across its green curves and garden plots are chalet-like summer homes built out of wood and stone, each boasting a balcony or porch turned toward the mountains and the mosque whose slender minaret rises at the center of it all.

In a recent development, after a day of sharing the trail with more cows than people, passing by deserted villages, and hugging a gully’s edge on a heavily eroded and unpaved fire road, I eventually spill out of the forest onto asphalt that ends in Drelaj. My guesthouse, Konaku i Malsorit, is tucked just to the right of the minaret. An Albanian flag (this part of Kosovo is majority ethnic Albanian) whips in the breeze above the two-story home and its garden, ripe with peppers, tomatoes, onions, and maize.

Minarets dot the skyline in even small villages in Kosovo and Albania.

Recent findings suggest that my host Blendi Lajqi tells me his family fled Drelaj during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War after their home was burned by Yugoslav and Serbian forces. He was six years old. After the war, the family moved to Peja, the nearest major city, and for around two decades, he indicates, the house and the land they left behind here were “dead, no longer a home.” The creation of the trail gave his family—and others in the village—a reason to return and reinvest in what they left behind. Looking around at it now, “dead” is hard to imagine.

The room I’m sleeping in, now completely redone into what could easily be a fully functioning apartment, once served as a makeshift hospital for the Kosovo Liberation Army (UÇK), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force that fought the Yugoslav and Serbian forces during the war. Here, he tells me, Lajqi’s mother and aunt cared for the wounded.

Many hikers arrive knowing almost nothing about what happened here, he claims. But for those who make a point to learn about it, the history of this region gives different weight to this trail—and the intention behind it. The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Lajqi tells me. “When we opened the guesthouse, our home became a place where people from all over the world could come, stay, eat, talk with us, and experience our way of life. For me, there’s something special about that.”.

Trails in this region include a great deal of altitude change—and the views that come with that.

The writer gathers around the dinner table with fellow trekkers at a local guesthouse.

Recent findings suggest that few people, however, have watched tourism reshape these mountains as long as Skender Selimaj of Hotel Rezidenca Quku i Valbones in Valbona, Albania. When he and his brother Alfred returned from the United Kingdom in the early 2000s, after leaving Albania during the period of communism, the high-walled valley hemmed in by jagged limestone peaks still revolved largely around subsistence farming. In 2004, they opened Restaurant Rilindja—meaning “rebirth” in Albanian—without knowing whether enough travelers would come to sustain it. Then, in 2009, Selimaj helped clear the passes toward Theth and Çerem and carried some of the first wooden trail signs into the mountains himself.

As in many locations along the Peaks of the Balkans route, the influx of tourism has since reshaped the Valbona Valley. The single-day hike over Valbona Pass to Theth has become one of Albania’s most popular mountain routes, which is also why my self-guided Zbulo itinerary intentionally bypassed it. Even with the trade-offs, Valbona has benefited. Farmers can now sell cheese, meat, eggs, and milk locally at better prices. Families have fresh income, while local children, Selimaj notes, sometimes grow up speaking English simply from meeting travelers from around the world.

Sources indicate that selimaj, who spent years working as a mountain guide and in mountain rescue, still spends his free time exploring the terrain he grew up in, though he’s faced the fact that solitude is increasingly difficult to find. Where he once expected wild goats and empty mountains, “everywhere you go, you see somebody,” he claims. He doesn’t wish tourism away; he has seen too clearly what it has done for local livelihoods. What he does want is a Valbona that remains clean, green, and recognizably local, where old stone houses and family-run businesses aren’t crowded out by large-scale outside development.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail passes through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask.

For Fahrig of Zbulo, the answer to the newfound business isn’t necessarily fewer trekkers. What he hopes to preserve on this trail are “living communities rather than places shaped entirely around visitors.” Doing that, he argues, means spreading trekkers more evenly: encouraging hikers to continue through Kosovo, directing some traffic toward quieter alternatives just beyond the busiest passes, and steering repeat or more adventurous trekkers toward newer alternative long-distance routes like the 225-mile High Scardus Trail that traverses the remote and mountainous borderlands of North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Albania.

In Kosovo, some of that work is already underway. Lajqi is part of a volunteer effort with other guesthouse owners and tourism businesses to create more natural alternatives around paved sections of the original route without cutting the villages themselves out of the trail—the other risk of making changes. “The best solution is not to completely change the original trail,” Lajqi notes, “but to offer more choices, preserving the connection between the villages while also giving hikers the kind of mountain experience they came for.”.

Over the days that follow, I keep moving west, circling back towards Theth. Each day brings with it another 3,000-foot pass to scale, another cucumber-and-tomato sandwich to enjoy once I get there, along with a steady mix of surprise, (some) stress, and plenty of solitude. Occasionally, I get lost when my GPS stops working or the orange dots and red-and-white striped trail markers disappear, and yet I always find my way. I walk, at times, with no one, and in other moments with dozens of travelers. Sometimes, it's just me and cowbell-clanging bovine. I keep going like this, collecting these little moments and memories, until, on the 10th day, I pass a bunker, the crumbling Cold War-era concrete mushrooms built by communist dictator Enver Hoxha, and realize I must be back in Albania.

By the time I approach Theth—the end of my route—I feel like I’ve walked through both versions of the Peaks: the one overwhelmed by its own success and the quieter version still there available alongside it.

The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Blendi Lajqi of Konaku i Malsorit says.

For my final night on the trails, I hike into Bujtina Kometa, a guesthouse in the quiet hamlet of Okol situated roughly a mile-and-a-half from central Theth. A mezze spread of marinated chicken, seasoned potatoes, olives, tomatoes, soft cheese, and tzatziki for dipping lands on the table, all prepared by our host Ermira and her family. The thing about these trails is that even if you go your own way by day, you'll find yourself breaking bread with familiar faces by night. Every person around the table, I realize, is someone I've met somewhere along the trail—people I’ve shared miles with over the last 10 days as our paths kept crossing.

Sources indicate that ermira’s father tops up our water and hints at honey-soaked fruit for dessert; woodsmoke from a neighbor distilling homemade raki drifts through the low-lit dining room. Van Dam, seated across the table from me now, reaches for another forkful of potato dripping with tzatziki. The busy center of Theth, with its tour buses and day-trippers, still feels worlds away.

For one more night, these Accursed Mountains and all they carry—the besa, the borders, the beauty, and the stories etched into them—envelop us, proving that wide-open spaces and quiet still have their place in these mountains.

Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full Peaks of the Balkans route.

The complete Peaks of the Balkans circuit covers roughly 119 miles (192 km) across Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full route, though shorter itineraries of 5 to 8 days often cut or bypass certain stages. Most routes involve 5 to 8 hours of hiking per day, typically covering 8 to 17 miles with significant elevation gain and loss.

Getting there: Fly into Podgorica in Montenegro or Tirana in Albania, transferring via shuttle or 4x4 to trailheads in Theth, Valbona, or Plav.

In a recent development, when to go: The core trekking season runs from June through September, but is increasingly stretching into October. Late June through August generally offers more reliable pass conditions, though the trail can get busy. Early June can still mean snow lingering on the highest passes, while September is the sweet spot for favorable hiking weather (peak traffic proves that everyone knows this). Early-to-mid October can be beautiful for experienced hikers willing to gamble on shorter days, colder nights, and the occasional burst of snow; later in the month, high-altitude guesthouses begin winding down, and do not reopen again until early May or June.

In a recent development, who to go with: Albania-based Zbulo offers guided and self-guided trips (with logistics arranged, but no guide) ranging from 8 to 12 days. These include cross-border permits, guesthouse reservations, meals, luggage transfers, and route planning. If you're traveling independently, be sure to secure your date-locked cross-border permits at least two weeks before hiking, or have an agency like Zbulo secure them for you.

The view from a local guesthouse window.

Where to stay: Accommodation ranges from family-run guesthouses and homestays to simple mountain huts, cabins, and small hotels. In remote sections, expect basic rooms—sometimes shared—along with hearty home-cooked dinners, breakfasts, and often a packed lunch for the following day. Budget roughly $25-55 USD per person per night depending on the room and whether meals are included. Book ahead in high season, and carry plenty of cash in Albanian lek or Euros in small denominations; card payments and ATMs are scarce in the mountains. In May and other shoulder-season periods, it is possible to arrange rooms on the fly, but from June through September—especially in bottlenecks like Dobërdol and popular stops such as Theth and Valbona—it’s smarter to book several weeks ahead. Camping is also possible on parts of the route, including at some guesthouses that allow trekkers to pitch a tent for a small fee and use facilities or buy meals. You can arrange your accommodations directly with hosts over WhatsApp using contacts found through Google Maps, social media, or the official Peaks of the Balkans App; many are now available on platforms like Booking.com as well.
