#30672. Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

📅 23 Apr 2021 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1478 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Dreaming of Country Living? These Renovated Barn Airbnbs Got You Covered

📅 23 Apr 2021 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path.
  • Sources indicate that from sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country.
  • Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that country living, with its beautiful nature, relaxing atmosphere, and stunning wildlife, makes it incredibly easy to forget your day-to-day stressors and embrace the slower path. And where better to enjoy this peace and quiet than from an Airbnb converted from a barn—provided, of course, you’re not actually sleeping next to a pitchfork and a pile of hay? Across the US, old dairy barns, horse stables, haylofts, and grain silos that once kept America’s farms running are finding dreamy second lives as vacation rentals. These sturdy structures are getting some very glamorous redesigns, but keeping the soaring ceilings, original timber beams, weathered wood, and old architectural details that no fresh build can quite replicate.

Sources indicate that from sprawling farmhouses with enough room for the whole gang, to intimate hayloft hideaways made for a national park trip, to old grain silos that are surprisingly stylish places to sleep, there’s something interesting in every corner of the country. Expect modern interiors tucked behind century-old barn doors, outdoor soaking tubs overlooking rolling pastures, and properties where the resident animals are still very much part of the picture (morning coffee with a few curious goats, anyone?).

Whether you’re after a little farmyard nostalgia, a design-forward country escape, or simply a storied home just steps away from the wild, these barn Airbnbs make a pretty compelling case to trade your average stay for something with a little more hay-day history.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to Nashville, floor-to-ceiling windows, fully equipped kitchen, optional farm tours and event bookings.

Bloomsbury Farm is a family-owned and -operated organic farm just outside Nashville. The 400-acre retreat is pastorally posh—the kind of place where wild turkeys and deer roam free, hawks swoop overhead, and coyotes howl in the night. The one-bedroom, one-bath rental is tastefully decorated: It’s where Martha Stewart meets Modern Farmer. That remarked, intentionality permeates every design choice, from the handsome leather headboard to the subway-tiled bath with Aesop hand soap. Guests are given farm-fresh eggs and a box of fruits and vegetables that are grown on-site; these come in handy when preparing meals on the kitchen’s professional gas range or grilling over the outdoor firepit.

City: Smyrna, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Brewer Farms, Cedar Stone Park, The Barn at Sycamore Farms, Arrington Vineyards.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Proximity to NYC, wood-burning fireplace, reading nooks, meadow and valley views, vintage arcade and board games.

Just around a two-hour drive from NYC, this charmingly restored barn cottage awaits in the Hudson Valley. The space pairs a cozy wood-burning fireplace with expansive windows overlooking a meadow—one that the host notes becomes a “veritable bird sanctuary for most of the year.” It’s a harbor of hidden nooks made for cozying up with a book, and features a well-stocked kitchen and dining space for cooking, as well as a vintage arcade and board games for fun nights in with your crew. Previous guests have raved about its proximity to Hudson Valley hot spots: There’s no shortage of places to hike, ski, see art, or dine, as well as some fun local breweries and wineries. The property is within a 10- to 25-minute drive of six quaint Hudson Valley towns. (You can also request bikes from the hosts if you’re inclined to venture out on two wheels.).

City: Red Hook, New YorkThings to do nearby: Pine Plains, Stissing Mountain (and iconic restaurant Stissing House), Thompson Pond.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Desert views, on-site animals, proximity to Zion National Park, fully equipped kitchen, firepit, sauna.

Industry observers note that with a classic red-barn build, friendly farm animals, and a sauna practically made for stargazing, this dreamy Airbnb is an oasis—especially if Zion National Park is on your itinerary. Just one hour from the park, you’ll find this whimsical base for two set between Utah’s red rock cliffs, sweeping canyons, and heaps of local hiking paths. Inside, enjoy tasteful touches everywhere. Sunlight pours through the studio; a vintage-style soaking tub sits on black-and-white checkered flooring, and the kitchenette has modern appliances as well as some plants and pastel green cabinets. You’ll have some company when walking outside, too: This farm stay comes with two adorable Highland cows as well as a chicken coop. There’s also a sauna and firepit, just in case you need another reason to visit.

City: Hildale, UtahThings to do nearby: Water Canyon Winery, Squirrel Canyon Trailhead, Coral Pink Sand Dunes, Zion National Park.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Outdoor firepit, central location, private stargazing deck, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl player.

A silo in the Catskills? Now that's a fun place to spend a weekend. From the outside, this three-story converted tower is fairly understated, but step inside, and you'll find a surprisingly airy, thoughtfully designed little escape that makes every inch count. There's an open living room that flows into a stocked kitchen, two spacious (and stunningly modern) bathrooms, and a private deck for soaking up the quiet. The interiors have a cool, pared-back feel, with just the right amount of personality to make it feel like somewhere you'd actually want to hang out (board games and a puzzle marathon are very much encouraged). And while it feels nicely tucked away, Woodstock's galleries, shops, and restaurants are just 10 minutes down the road.

City: Willow, Newly introduced YorkThings to do nearby: Mount Tremper, Emerson Kaleidoscope, Phoenicia Diner, Overlook Mountain.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ocean views, stereo system, heated floors, wood-burning stove, open and modern kitchen.

It has been revealed that what could be better—or more endearing—than this modern Northern California barn in a forest clearing? Renovated by San Francisco architect David Crimmins, this gem leans into its sleek agrarian style, with airy, open-beam ceilings, heated concrete floors, a redwood slab dining table, and windows on all sides, bringing the outside in. The house sits along a rocky coastline, primed for whale watching and trips to coastal wineries between the Redwoods and the Pacific. The high-design stay stands tall on Anchor Bay along the Mendocino Coast; you’ll have your very own one-acre yard amid the state’s dreamy Redwoods, and it’s just a 20-minute walk to the beach.

City: Gualala, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Whale Watch Point, Gualala Arts Center, Point Arena Lighthouse, Bonham Trail to Cooks Beach.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, outdoor shower, proximity to Lake Michigan.

In a recent development, not every barn stay comes with Lake Michigan practically in its backyard. Tucked among 12 wooded acres in Leelanau County, this country base holds its former farm structure while offering its guests a fresh and pretty new lease. Once part of a 30-acre farm that stretched across both sides of the road, you can still appreciate a little of that history in its beautifully restored bones. These days, it's a two-bedroom hideaway that makes a wonderful home base for exploring Northern Michigan's wine country, with Northport's small-town charm and the peninsula's wineries and breweries just a hop and a skip away. There’s no need to leave your Airbnb for a fun day out: Spend the afternoon wandering out in nature, then make your way to the nearby secluded Lake Michigan beach. Peruse the guest reviews, and you’ll notice a telling pattern: Most travelers don't just stay once or twice—they return time and time again.

City: Northport, MichiganThings to do nearby: Cherry Basket Farm, Onomonee Road Beach, Fischer’s Happy Hour Tavern, Bay Front Park.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Silo design, mountain views, fully equipped kitchenette, private patio, firepit, proximity to Glacier National Park.

Sources indicate that on an 80-acre family farm in Montana’s Flathead Valley, this converted grain silo is truly one of a kind. Alongside jaw-dropping mountain views, the structure itself is a treat—and happens to be more homey than one might think at first glance. Inside, the lofted king bedroom is spacious and comfy, the kitchenette is stocked with all you might need for a long weekend, and kid-friendly amenities are at your ready, from a pack-and-play to a portable high chair. That stated, it’s best for one or two, or a couple traveling with a little one, since there aren’t full walls between the sleeping area.

Embrace the outdoors as much as you can here: According to previous guests, this barn puts you in a prime spot for stargazing around the firepit, jumping in the glittering Flathead Lake, and taking advantage of Glacier National Park—only 30 minutes away.

City: Kalispell, MontanaThings to do nearby: Glacier National Park, Conrad Mansion Museum, Flathead Lake, Wild Horse Island.

Introduction: I Crossed The Atlantic Six Times So My Kids Could Spend A Month In Germany

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taking my kids to Germany for a month should have required one flight across the Atlantic and another flight home.
  • I realize I will certainly not win any accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language.
  • That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taking my kids to Germany for a month should have required one flight across the Atlantic and another flight home. Instead, getting them there, returning to the United States, flying back to pick them up, and inserting one especially circuitous journey along the way meant I crossed the Atlantic six times…including a memorable detour through Greenland.

I realize I will certainly not win any accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language. They are German citizens too after all. And so what I did this summer, as I did last summer and as I will do next summer, was take them over to Germany in mid-July and pick them up in mid-August.

That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.

I booked a round-trip economy class ticket in spring to get us home from our ski trip and then back in the summer, which included SWISS economy class ticket from Zurich – Chicago and Austrian economy class from Los Angeles – Zurich via Vienna and was even able to squeeze in an overnight in Vienna at the Park Hyatt, which I booked for 25,000 Hyatt points.

The week I booked (the last week in February) was the week the conflict in Iran broke out and I was very happy I booked when I did because I got the tickets for $764 r/t. I also booked before United cut off awarding mileage on basic economy tickets. Since I booked on United ticketing stock, I received PQPs (status points) and RDMs (redeemable miles) for these flights. I also figured the lack of advance seat assignments would not matter because I was traveling with two young children. That gamble paid off well and we were seated together at check-in on each flight.

That got us to Germany, but I had to find a way back to the USA and then back to Europe the following month to pick them up, plus a ticket home for all three of us.

Flying Blue came through with a perfectly-timed last minute 60K redemption on Air France from Basel – Paris – New York, plus €453 in taxes. It was such a pleasure to fly on Air France and I look forward to sharing all the details from my A350-900 business class flight.

Recall I landed in JFK around 10:00 pm and drove overnight to Pittsburgh, which itself was a journey. Then from there I flew home via Lisbon, Frankfurt, and Washington, DC…as one does.

But then I had to get from Southern California back to Basel and decided to fly via San Francisco, Denver, Newark, Nuuk (Greenland), and Copenhagen. That was three tickets, including:.

I found SAS Business Class saver award space to get the three of us back to the USA, which has to be one of the best deals out there at 60K EuroBonus miles for me and only 30K miles for the kids, which included business class from ZRH-CPH as well. Taxes were €214.59 total for the three of us.

The flight availability forced an overnight in Copenhagen, but a late arrival so we used 36,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to stay at the AC Hotel Bella Sky Copenhagen near the airport, a towering property that was perfect for the overnight layover.

I won’t review the JetBlue A220 flight to Burbank since we all fell asleep right away after too much Taco Bell in Times Square….

(plus I’ve reviewed it before here).

These are the segments for this trip report:.

I look forward to sharing this report with you!

    This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

    📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded.
    • And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.
    • As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

    And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

    As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

    Recent findings suggest that in the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

    But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

    Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

    And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

    The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up promptly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

    It has been revealed that as an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

    Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

    If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

    #30668. Jim Jordan picked as fresh minority leader for House GOP

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1193 w)

    Jim Jordan picked as fresh minority leader for House GOP

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep.
    • The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election.
    • “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

    The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

    “Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan noted after the hourslong process.

    In a recent development, the two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the latest Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

    “Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

    As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

    Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member stated: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”.

    The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

    Recent findings suggest that majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

    In a recent development, “We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran remarked Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”.

    “Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” remarked Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

    But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

    “To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he remarked at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

    Sources indicate that in the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

    “We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

    In a recent development, in the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

    But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

    It has been revealed that johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”.

    Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

    Sources indicate that democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Newly introduced York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

    It has been revealed that “It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”.

    Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

    In a recent development, the Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

    “It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, remarked in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”.

    According to recent reports, several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, remarked they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”.

    It has been revealed that the latest leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”.

    Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

    In a recent development, “Well, I did it for four years,” the president noted of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”.

    Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

    #30667. Tech Report: 14 best hotels in Australia 2026 worth travelling across the world for

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2936 w)

    Tech Report: 14 best hotels in Australia 2026 worth travelling across the world for

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that between the 37,000 miles worth of picturesque coastline, vast outback, vibrant cities and laidback locals, Australia is a bucket list mainstay for many.
    • Sources indicate that I woke up at the Park Hyatt Sydney to golden light pouring into my room through floor-to-ceiling windows.
    • Staying at Qualia is like stepping inside a James Bond film.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that between the 37,000 miles worth of picturesque coastline, vast outback, vibrant cities and laidback locals, Australia is a bucket list mainstay for many. Those who make the long haul flight are rewarded with many riches: koala cuddles, consistently balmy weather and the best coffee in the world. To make the journey even more worthwhile, Australia is home to numerous destination stays, from tropical islands to remote lodges and outback homestays, all offering incredible access to the country's most unique landscapes and wildlife. Dine in tree tops, swim with turtles or enjoy a front-row seat to Sydney's sweeping harbour. For more inspiration to add to your Down Under trip, these are some of the best hotels in Australia according to our editors.

    Sources indicate that I woke up at the Park Hyatt Sydney to golden light pouring into my room through floor-to-ceiling windows. I stepped out onto a balcony – one of two – and watched the metropolis wake up: the ships and ferries coming into the harbor, good-looking Sydneysiders out for their morning run on the boardwalk, the sun rising behind that iconic sail-shaped opera house. From its prime spot in the Rocks historic neighbourhood on the western side of Sydney Cove, the hotel has offered a front-row seat to this Aussie scene for the past 35 years. That’s 35 Latest Year’s Eve fireworks displays that the Park Hyatt’s extremely lucky guests have seen from this vantage point: fountains of sparks and chrysanthemums of light bursting from both the Sydney Opera House and Harbour Bridge, all ringing in another 365 days of good fortune. And there I stood on an ordinary Wednesday in September, in a plush bathrobe, sipping on a demitasse of espresso and wishing over a pale blue sky the same for myself. I was so happy to mark the occasion of my first work anniversary at this hotel. Sure, I could chalk it up to its large and sumptuously appointed rooms, its team’s attentive service, or its fresh and delicious brekkies that lend credence to the belief that Australians invented avocado toast. But as they say: location, location, location. No matter the occasion, a stay at the Park Hyatt Sydney, I’d venture, gives you the feeling of being exactly where you should be. Matt Ortile.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Staying at Qualia is like stepping inside a James Bond film. Helicopters whisk you away to the Great Barrier Reef or a private island championship golf course. Meanwhile, those with vertigo can cruise by Whitsunday Beach on a 75-foot yacht instead. That is, of course, if you decide to leave the resort at all. Qualia’s 63 villas are scattered atop a secluded hillside on the northern tip of Hamilton Island, overlooking the Coral Sea. The studio-style Leeward Pavilions face the south — ideal for sunset — and the larger Windward Pavilions feature a plunge pool, living room, and bathtub with an epic waterfront backdrop. (Windward Pavilion #6 is the quietest sanctuary.) The two main restaurants include the treetop Long Pavilion, where breakfast is a standout, and the poolside Pebble Beach, which transforms from a light Mediterranean lunch to a romantic, multi-course dinner in the evening. Perhaps the most impressive is the concierge, who customises one-of-a-kind itineraries for each guest and delivers seamless, top-notch service. Chelsea Bengier.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    Located 120 miles north of Cairns, secluded on 1,000 hectares of tawny bush, and ringed by sugar-white beaches, Lizard Island is no hard sell. It’s one of the few luxury resorts in Australia with the bragging rights to being located directly on the Great Barrier Reef. An easy 10-minute snorkel from shore will reveal the alternate, neon-tinged universe of the fringing reef. Silvery slivers of fish reflect the bright Queensland light, and slo-mo turtles glide above gardens of giant purple clams and coral that’s shaped like uncooked spaghetti. There is as much to do underwater – diving, fishing, swimming – as above. Unfussy white-weatherboard villas, with still-wet swimsuits dripping upon timber decks, dot the island. Inside, the rooms are bright and airy and boast high ceilings. Some have with wide-frame views out onto the lapping blue sea, while others are wrapped in a garden that vibrates with scuttling critters. Out of sight, on its own jagged outcrop of granite rocks, is The House, a brutalist concrete and copper three-bedroom private villa, which is surrounded by lonely swaths of white-sand beach. But beyond the island’s obvious charms, it’s the Lizard Island Research Station – headed by a husband and wife duo – that really sets this place apart. Opened in 1973, the station is one of the world's leading reef-research facilities on a luxury resort, which guests can tour (even though it’s not part of the resort) – and they do, quizzing the marine scientists and even rolling up their sleeves to take part in hands-on citizen science initiatives across the endangered reef. It’s an insight into Australia’s changing relationship with tourism and proves that a remote paradise can be both beauty and brains. Chloe Sachdev.

    According to recent reports, the sandstone building that houses Fullerton Hotel Sydney was built more than 150 years ago and served for decades as the city’s General Post Office. It’s a building with real gravitas, and staying here feels like an event. The 516 rooms and suites are exercises in restraint, with a white-and-beige palette, generous floor space, and minimal furnishings. Well-stocked minibars, international television channels, and in-room coffee machines help ease the jet lag. The restaurant, The Place, draws guests and locals alike with a Southeast Asian – inflected menu and decadent desserts, while the bar occupies a corner of the grand atrium. Step outside and you’re on Martin Place, a pedestrianised plaza overlooked by grand old buildings housing Sydney’s substantial banks. The harbour is about 20 minutes’ walk and there are several train stations nearby. A branch of the city’s favourite ice-cream purveyor, Messina, is just across the road, as are fashion boutiques and upscale dining options. Dan F. Stapleton.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    According to recent reports, at this hotel on the pandanus-lined beachfront of Cabarita, the signature cocktail made with local Ink Gin changes from deep blue into shades of dusty pink. It completes the photographic panorama of navy and white sun beds, oversized sun hats, and bronzed pool boys. It’s here, in this lazy coastal pocket halfway between the Gold Coast and Byron Bay, that the linen-clad set come to kick back on long, hot summer days. Among the 21 rooms by Brisbane designer Anna Spiro, no two are the same. Each is a revision in 1960s eclecticism, with brass fixtures, antique memorabilia, and dark wood furniture whimsically combined with a Mediterranean sensibility of patterned floor tiles, starched linens, and wall panelling. Bathers migrate from the pool to dinner at Paper Daisy, the hotel’s restaurant helmed by Noma alum Ben Devlin, to try flavours of the surrounding landscape. For breakfast there are kefir pancakes with macadamia cream, passionfruit and berries, and lunches of prawn sandwiches with iceberg lettuce and avocado. A Moroccan-accented day spa with a domed hammam-style steam room was added in 2017. But it is perhaps general manager Mauro De Riso, with his charming sense of Italian hospitality, that stands out as the greatest investment made by owners Elisha and Siobhan Bickle. This boutique seaside bolthole etches a new, more sophisticated vision of the Australian lifestyle of surf, sun and sand on to the scene. John Hannan.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    My stay at El Questro Homestead, a cattle station turned luxury property, would end up being not much longer than the journey to reach it. Regardless of the length of my visit, nowhere else could I have experienced all that I did there. This member of Luxury Lodges of Australia has 10 rooms and suites on a clifftop overlooking the Chamberlain River. As part of a 2022 Indigenous Land Use Agreement, the traditional Ngarinyin landowners regained more than 400,000 acres of the property in a historic arrangement that El Questro’s owners say will make it possible to increase Indigenous employment. Many aspects of a stay at El Questro, however, will remain unchanged: in the morning screeching cockatoos act as an alarm clock. In the evening you can sit and watch crocodiles in the waters below. Later, a tree frog may hop its way into your bathroom. Four-wheel drive safaris and helicopter tours will take you to remote waterfalls and hot springs, and here, in one of the most sparsely inhabited regions in the world, new animal and plant species are discovered regularly. I happened to be standing next to a ranger when he came upon what appeared to be a new species of beetle. But I was even more impressed by Injiid Marlabu Calls Us, an immersive experience developed by traditional owners Mary and Nelson O’Reeri and their daughter Shonelle. The family recounts how Nelson's grandmother Injiid grew up on this land and how it was taken away from her by cattle barons; how her son was forced into a state home; and how she found him again decades later. To listen is to learn about the challenges and hopes that life holds for many Aboriginal people today. You will likely be deeply moved, and it may prove to be one of the most lasting memories of your visit. Dennis Braatz.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that when the catastrophic “black summer” bushfires of 2020 burnt down Southern Ocean Lodge, many thought it was the end of the story for one of Australia’s greatest luxury lodges. A fixture on Kangaroo Island’s sensational stretch of wild southwest coast, the resort was originally opened in 2008 by husband-and-wife duo James and Hayley Baillie, and it quickly became the soft-landing of choice to explore the “Australian Galápagos.” This story received a much-welcomed plot twist in December 2023, when the resort reopened as a near replica of its former sci-fi self, shaped like a low-flying saucer hovering above the Southern Ocean, with uninterrupted last-stop-before-Antarctica views across the sea. The resort now comprises 25 glass-fronted suites that extend across the limestone cliffs, each with midcentury-modern curves, sunken living rooms, fireplaces, and sliding doors that open to private patios and the fresh Antarctic breeze. On the western edge of the lodge, the four-bedroom Baillie Pavilion suite is a upcoming addition – it sits like an amphitheater with an infinity pool, a plunge pool/spa, and views across the coastal cliffs. Another tweak is the now north-facing spa, complete with a chill-out lounge, small gym, sauna, three treatment rooms, and hot and cold plunge pools. The reoriented spa turns its back to the sea to give guests a glimpse of the 250 acres of nature reserve surrounding the resort, all while they’re being massaged and scrubbed with the island’s bounty of lavender, eucalyptus, and pure Ligurian honey. Chloe Sachdev.

    Check Availability at Michelin Guide.

    This spot overlooking the Mossman River in the heart of the lush Daintree Rainforest, the world’s oldest tropical rainforest, has been special ever since it opened in the 1980s. But its 2021 makeover by Baillie Lodges – the Australian brand that specialises in show-stopping properties in remote locations – has elevated it to a whole different level, with the help of Sydney design team Pike Withers. Many of the 40 suites resemble decadent treehouses of polished hardwoods, with stone bathtubs on forest-fringed terraces. The hero lodging is the two-bedroom, 3,400-square-foot Daintree Pavilion, a contemporary jungle hide with a tiered horizon pool and extensive decking to capture every possible perspective of the surrounding rainforest, which was recently returned to its original custodians, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people. Everything here is geared towards total immersion in nature and culture – from tapping into local walking tours, on which Kuku Yalanji guides share ancient survival techniques, to Asian-inflected dinners in the soaring, cantilevered Treehouse Restaurant, high in the tropical canopy. At the Healing Waters Spa, the signature Ulysses face and body treatment features a mud bath and Vichy shower overlooking the rainforest. The spa is based on ancient ideas about the Mossman River as a life-giving force – reinforcing the sense that a deep connection to nature is everything here. Kendall Hill.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    According to recent reports, A Herculean effort is already required to travel to Australia from nearly everywhere else in the world. Then add an extra hour’s flight to Tasmania and a three-hour, serpentine drive from Hobart – during which doubt will inevitably creep in as to whether this could possibly be worth it. Relief sets in as this retreat’s main lodge comes into focus, with its modern, undulating roof and glass walls that bring the outside in. On the fringes of one of the island state’s oldest national parks, there are 20 sleek, villa-style rooms that stud the coastal bushland sloping down towards Great Oyster Bay and the craggy Hazards mountains beyond. Each one looks onto the water. It’s the kind of view that lures the staunchest night owl out of bed at 5am to watch the sunrise turn the bay a mercurial pink-silver. And there’s more to do once awake, such as kayaking on Pelican Bay while birds swoop overhead, fly-fishing for red spinners on Lake Leake, and visiting the nearby oyster farm to pluck, shuck, and slurp on the spot. At supper, chef Iain Todd – cooking almost exclusively with Tasmanian ingredients, including ones from his own garden, and seafood caught within sight of the hotel. Mark Ellwood.

    Check Availability at Michelin Guide.

    A fitting emblem of the fresh Perth, The Treasury is part of the ambitious Cathedral Square development, a $580 million reinvention of a cluster of 19th-century state treasury and Anglican Diocese buildings on the edge of the Central Business District, which sat empty for more than 20 years before the COMO outpost moved in. Almost every detail in the hotel (which primarily occupies the top floors of three 140-year-old buildings) has been returned to its original state, from the reinstalled dormer windows to the roofline’s copper trim. Check out Wildflower, the hotel's glassed-in rooftop restaurant, for a taste of this pioneer city's thriving food scene, courtesy of executive chef Kim Brennan, and David Thompson’s Thai street-food joint, Long Chim, adjacent to the hotel. Todd Plummer.

    Discover luxury and natural beauty when you stay at InterContinental Hayman Great Barrier Reef, a private island resort with multiple restaurants, spa and gym facilities, and myriad experiences to partake in. Your days can be adrenaline-filled with water activities like jet-skiing, snorkelling, and fishing, or simply relaxing poolside with meals punctuating your day. The design is minimalist with beachy motifs, and the property offers a wide variety of room options from courtyard rooms to sprawling residences. Hayman Island has been renowned for its hospitality for decades—it’s a well-oiled machine, whether you’re seeking a vacation filled with adventures or unwinding at the spa. Rana Good.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that set on Hobart’s historic Hunter Street wharf, The Henry Jones Art Hotel is an elegant waterfront stay in Australia’s first dedicated art hotel, a romantic, non-stuffy converted 19th-century warehouse with local art, history tours, and a Tasmanian restaurant anchored by a custom asado grill. The 56-room hotel features more than 400 pieces of shoppable art selected by full-time curator Kate Jackson and representing roughly 70 to 80 Tasmanian artists. Each room is unique, blending industrial past with modern finishes, exposed timber beams, original brick and sandstone, and walls layered with Tasmanian artwork. Landscape Restaurant & Grill is a highlight, with seasonal ingredients from more than 20 Tasmanian farmers and producers. The hotel’s prime central location is a major perk, with Salamanca, Constitution Dock, and the ferry for MONA an easy stroll away. What’s not to miss is the complimentary art or history tour, which turns the hotel from a boutique stay into a portal to Hobart’s history and contemporary creative culture. Kaila Yu.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    As face-lifts go, the $40 million spent to transform this 1891 Melbourne grand dame into a cool city chick has proved to be well spent. Today, although the five-story Rialto is dwarfed by its skyscraper neighbors, it exudes charm on the outside and class within. On the National Heritage List, it is actually two buildings (the older, Gothic Rialto and the Romanesque Winfield Building) linked by a soaring glass ceiling that covers what was once a wide lane. The King suites and Deluxe rooms have all the expected mod cons, the wood-paneled roof-top pool and sauna drip with minimalist comfort, and the service is super-snappy. The real star, however, is the enormous atrium, a spectacle of light, angles, marble, mosaic, bluestone, and carefully selected local art. At its base is the Alluvial Restaurant, host to deal-making business-types and Rialto residents. Overlooking it is the Market Lane bar, with its deep leather couches and more than 100 kinds of martinis, including an antipodean array featuring everything from bloodlimes to quandongs.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Sources indicate that every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

    #30666. Trump Blames Biden For Nationwide FAA Meltdown But Union Points To Sloppy Contractor Work On His Watch

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1701 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump Blames Biden For Nationwide FAA Meltdown But Union Points To Sloppy Contractor Work On His Watch

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Trump administration wants Americans to blame Joe Biden for the nationwide FAA meltdown.
    • President Donald Trump finally addressed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on Sunday morning.
    • “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Trump administration wants Americans to blame Joe Biden for the nationwide FAA meltdown. But the union representing FAA safety specialists points to a far more immediate failure: contractor maintenance performed in the middle of the day without the risk assessment and federal oversight historically used for such work. Separate questions surrounding a large FAA technology contract and a political contribution to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s son-in-law also deserve a careful look, though the evidence does not appear to connect that system to the outage.

    President Donald Trump finally addressed Friday’s nationwide ground stop on Sunday morning. Rather than apologize to travelers or promise an independent investigation, he blamed the previous administration:.

    “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Massive money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began. We have the knowledge and plan for the Flight Control Systems, we need Congress to give the money, FAST! Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.”.

    He followed that with another demand for congressional funding:.

    “If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built swiftly and efficiently. It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old – RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve. The Biden Administration set it back years!”.

    There is plenty of blame to distribute across multiple administrations. The air traffic control system is dangerously old, and the Biden administration did not solve that problem during its four years in power. It also experienced its own nationwide ground stop in January 2023 after the NOTAM system failed.

    In a recent development, but the telecommunications network did not suddenly become antiquated when Biden entered office. Congress and administrations from both parties have tolerated obsolete FAA infrastructure for decades, including Trump during his first term.

    More importantly, Friday’s failure occurred in November 2026, nearly two years into Trump’s second term, while a federal contractor was performing work under the supervision of the current FAA, not the Biden FAA.

    Blaming Biden does not explain what happened, full stop.

    The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS), which represents approximately 11,000 FAA employees, has offered a much more specific criticism. According to the union, the problem was isolated to two contractor-owned and maintained routers being updated during the middle of the day.

    Industry observers note that PASS indicates that contractors have historically followed a process in which FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance. Its technicians were not involved in the work that preceded Friday’s ground stop. The union explained:.

    “Historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.”.

    That raises an obvious question: why was that process not followed here?

    Industry observers note that while the union stops short of saying that a FAA risk assessment would definitely have prevented the failure, risk assessments exist precisely because even routine work can produce extraordinary consequences when performed on critical infrastructure. If federal technicians had historically provided another layer of review before this sort of work, excluding them deserves a much better explanation than the blame game we have received from current leaders.

    Duffy disputes the implication that PASS technicians were improperly sidelined.

    Industry observers note that appearing on CBS, he argued that union technicians work on FAA-owned radios, radar equipment, and other systems, while L3Harris owns and maintains the telecommunications network involved here. He said contractors have performed this sort of work thousands of times and maintained that the process was handled appropriately.

    Industry observers note that that’s true, but the union did not claim that its members ordinarily install L3Harris routers. It claimed FAA employees historically performed a risk assessment and coordinated the maintenance before contractors worked on the equipment.

    Those are different functions, right?

    It has been revealed that duffy’s explanation that the contractor owns the network does not answer whether FAA personnel should evaluate the operational risk of changing equipment that can destabilize communications and radar feeds across the entire National Airspace System. The FAA’s own questions and answers page acknowledges that the agency will reevaluate when this sort of maintenance is performed.

    The FAA states data flooded the network at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Investigators are examining a new router installed by L3Harris at a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as well as equipment at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas (amazing, isn’t it, that a simple router revision in Arkansas and Texas could cripple air traffic control across the USA?).

    The agency stabilized the network by blocking those locations and disabling the relevant broadcasting function on approximately 60 similar routers.

    It has been revealed that so yes, the older network was vulnerable. But the immediate event was not simply “old equipment.” It occurred during maintenance involving a new router connected to that old network. That brings us back to planning, testing, oversight, and timing.

    Industry observers note that > Read More: What Caused The FAA Meltdown? Duffy And Mullin Give Different Accounts.

    There is another issue circulating online involving Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the Boston technology organization developing the FAA’s upcoming Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART.

    For the avoidance of doubt: SMART did not cause Friday’s outage.

    The FAA says SMART is a data aggregator that does not feed information into the air traffic control system. ASI has likewise denied that its technology or FAA integration played any role. There appears to be no connection between SMART and the failed L3Harris telecommunications equipment.

    The fact that SMART expanded nationwide three days before the ground stop naturally attracted attention. Timing alone, however, does not establish causation. Calling ASI “the AI startup involved in the flight chaos” is therefore misleading based on the evidence presently available…there’s plenty of fodder without drawing links that do not exist.

    But ASI’s federal contract and political spending still merit scrutiny on their own terms. According to federal spending records, the FAA awarded ASI a contract on June 23, 2026, with a potential value of $875.95 million through 2038 (that is the contract ceiling, not money already paid to the firm. Approximately $23.34 million has been obligated so far).

    Federal Election Commission records also show that the Air Space Intelligence political action committee contributed $2,500 on March 31, 2026, to the congressional campaign of Michael Alfonso, Duffy’s son-in-law. Alfonso subsequently won election to represent Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District, the same seat Duffy once held.

    Industry observers note that there is no smoking gun that the contribution influenced the contract award, that Duffy intervened in the procurement, or that ASI received favorable treatment in exchange for political support. But the appearance is still unfortunate. A organization seeking an FAA contract potentially worth hundreds of millions of dollars should recognize the problem with its PAC donating to the transportation secretary’s son-in-law shortly before the award.

    Even when completely lawful, such contributions predictably create suspicion about whether access and family connections played a role and frankly warrant investigation by Congress (it should not be a Democrats vs Republicans issue). The government should be able to explain the procurement process, the competition involved, and the safeguards used to keep political relationships separate from contracting decisions.

    Duffy now wants Congress to provide another $50 billion for air traffic control modernization, which was $20 billion higher than his $30 billion request to Congress the day before the meltdown.

    He may be right that much more money is needed. But Friday’s failure also demonstrates why money alone cannot solve this problem. Would another $50 billion have prevented the meltdown on Friday? I don’t think so. And it also merits mentioning that the FAA has already been allocated $12.5 billion and only spent about $1 billion so far….

    Modernization itself introduces risk when old and fresh technology must operate together. That makes careful testing and coordination more vital, not less. The matter is not money, but proper testing and transitioning.

    Sources indicate that congress should demand a precise accounting of what failed, why maintenance was performed at that time, whether the usual risk assessment was skipped, and what will prevent a recurrence before writing another very large check. Their job is not only the power of the purse, but to provide accountability and careful manage the taxpayer dollars they have been entrusted to steward.

    Congress should also insist on transparency surrounding major technology contracts like the one awarded to ASI….

    It has been revealed that president Trump can blame Biden, and there is no question that the previous administration left behind an air traffic control system badly in need of modernization. But so did Trump 45, and Trump is president now. Sean Duffy runs the Department of Transportation now. The FAA and its contractors performed the work that immediately preceded this failure now. Trump’s criticism rings hollow and Americans are not buying it.

    According to recent reports, the ASI political contribution does not explain the outage, but does warrant more transparently. More importantly, the administration should explain why a contractor was updating critical telecommunications equipment during the day without the FAA risk assessment the union says was historically performed. It should disclose how major modernization contracts are awarded and insulated from political influence. And perhaps most importantly for this administration, it should stop treating every failure as another opportunity for self-congratulation and partisan blame.

    According to recent reports, americans can accept that replacing ancient technology will produce occasional setbacks. What they should not accept is an administration that asks for another $50 billion before candidly explaining how the system it already controls was allowed to fail. And even more fundamentally, Americans highlighted on November 3rd that they were tried of finger pointing and blame games. May the current administration finally realize that so the next two years are not totally wasted….

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.
    • Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day.
    • According to recent reports, house Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

    Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

    According to recent reports, house Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

    In a recent development, democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

    Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The upcoming map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

    Recent findings suggest that “Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto noted in a Nov. 4 statement.

    In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”.

    While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

    Review: Austrian Airlines 777-200ER Economy Class Los Angeles To Vienna

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that austrian Airlines is about as old-school as you can get on its 777-200ER, with my 11.5 hour economy class flight featuring plenty of food and efficient service, but an uncomfortable seat, oppressively warm cabin, and no Wi-Fi.
    • My children spend a month in Germany each summer and we kicked off their time with a flight to VIE and a night in Vienna.
    • This ticket was part of a round-trip economy class itinerary I booked several months earlier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that austrian Airlines is about as old-school as you can get on its 777-200ER, with my 11.5 hour economy class flight featuring plenty of food and efficient service, but an uncomfortable seat, oppressively warm cabin, and no Wi-Fi. Here’s my full review.

    My children spend a month in Germany each summer and we kicked off their time with a flight to VIE and a night in Vienna.

    This ticket was part of a round-trip economy class itinerary I booked several months earlier. The outbound journey was on SWISS from Zürich to Chicago, while the return brought us from Los Angeles to Zürich via Vienna on Austrian Airlines.

    In a recent development, the entire ticket cost $764 round-trip, which was an excellent fare. I booked through United Airlines before it stopped awarding redeemable miles and Premier qualifying points on basic economy tickets, so I still received credit for these flights.

    Recent findings suggest that the tradeoff was that advance seat assignments were not included. I was traveling with two young children, however, and correctly assumed we would be seated together at check-in. We received three adjacent seats without paying anything extra.

    I checked in online and we were traveling without larger baggage, so we showed up to LAX about 75 minutes prior to departure, breezed through security, and boarded our flight about 50 minutes before departure.

    I did stop briefly at the counter to see if we could be moved to a section of three (instead of the center section of four that we were auto-assigned) and I was obliged, which was fortunate since the flight ended up going out 100% full.

    Stepping onboard, we made our way to the rear economy class cabin for our long journey ahead.

    Austrian Airlines configures its Boeing 777-200ER with 330 seats: 32 in business class, 40 in premium economy, and 258 in economy class. Economy is arranged in a dense 3-4-3 configuration, with a minimum seat pitch of 30 inches.

    The cabin is dated with the dreary fluorescent light and smaller overhead bins, but was clean and well-maintained. Each Recaro seat included an adjustable headrest, a seatback entertainment screen, a low voltage USB-A port, a tray table, and a literature pocket. Glaringly, there are no power outlets for 110v/220v devices.

    Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, I did not find the seat particularly comfortable. Legroom felt very tight, especially when the passenger in front reclined, and the padding was not generous. Ten seats across on a Boeing 777 also makes for a narrow experience, though that has sadly become common throughout the industry.

    It has been revealed that A pillow and blanket were waiting at each seat. Both were perfectly respectable for economy class, but neither could overcome the larger problem: the cabin remained oppressively warm throughout the flight. I already struggle to sleep in economy class, and the combination of limited space and excessive heat eliminated any realistic chance of rest. There were no overhead air vents and it was just too warm onboard.

    In a recent development, my children had no such problem. They twisted themselves into positions that would leave me unable to walk for a week and slept for nearly eight hours. Oh, to be young….

    Austrian served dinner after takeoff, followed by a cold snack midway through the flight and a hot breakfast before landing in Vienna. Whatever else I may say about the quality, Austrian certainly did not leave passengers hungry.

    Service began with a crackers and drinks (all alcohol was free and I had a glass of prosecco).

    It has been revealed that dinner choices were chicken or pasta. I chose the chicken, which consisted of four large breaded pieces that looked a bit like Wiener schnitzel. It was served with potatoes, green beans, a salad, bread, and cake.

    Austrian posts its economy class menus online:.

    SEASONAL LETTUCE with balsamic vinaigrette.

    FRIED CHICKEN TENDER with steamed potatoes.

    CHEESE TORTELLINI with tomato-basil sauce and parmesan.

    The portion was enormous for economy class. My children could not finish their meals, but I managed to eat mine and then finished theirs…plenty of protein on this flight.

    The chicken was also the popular choice throughout the cabin. Flight attendants ran out a couple of rows behind us, leaving passengers in the rear portion of economy class with pasta as their only option, making me very thankful we were not seated further back.

    A cold cheese sandwich was distributed midway through the flight that was not wort eating (highly processed American bread and cheese).

    I appreciated that Austrian served a second hot meal before landing, not that it was worth eating either. Breakfast included an omelet with mushrooms, potatoes, and a tomato. Unfortunately, the omelet tasted artificial and powdery, while the mushrooms underneath it were repulsive. I’m not expecting fresh eggs like Lufthansa First Class, but this was a really poor-quality breakfast.

    Coffee was another disappointment. Austrian is famous for its elaborate coffee menu in business class, including specialties like the Wiener Melange, but economy class passengers received powdered coffee. Yuck. I do not expect barista-quality coffee in economy class, but surely an Austrian flag carrier can provide freshly brewed filter coffee on a longhaul flight. The powdered substitute was horrible. Alright, I’ll stop griping….

    Each economy class seat had a personal touchscreen entertainment system with movies, television programs, music, games, and a moving map. The interface and screen looked dated compared to the latest systems, including on the Austrian 787 Dreamliners, and the overall selection was more limited than what you will find on U.S. and Gulf carriers.

    In a recent development, even so, my children had no trouble finding enough content to keep themselves occupied before sleeping…that is ultimately what mattered most on this flight. Headphones were provided, though passengers who care about sound quality should bring their own (as my children did).

    Industry observers note that that is increasingly difficult to excuse on an intercontinental aircraft in 2026. I can prepare for a flight without connectivity, and I had done so here, but an 11.5-hour journey represents a substantial portion of the working day and it’s crazy that Austrian hasn’t even installed slow Wi-Fi while its competitors are offering Starlink.

    Austrian will eventually replace its aging Boeing 777 fleet with Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, but until then, passengers on these aircraft should plan to remain offline throughout the flight and Austrian just confirmed these 777s will remain until the end of 2029 or early 20230.

    Service was efficient and professional throughout the flight.

    The crew completed multiple meal and beverage services, distributed water during the journey, and collected trays promptly. While not especially warm or memorable, service competent and orderly.

    With a full economy class cabin and several meal services to complete, the flight attendants worked continuously. Our interactions were brief, but everything we needed was provided…no complaints.

    My children were offered colored pencils, paper, and a matching game.

    As I eluded to above, the greatest problem on this flight was the temperature.

    Sources indicate that the cabin remained oppressively warm for most of the flight. I find Lufthansa Group carriers frequently keep their cabins warmer than I prefer, but this flight was particularly uncomfortable. Passengers who feel cold can put on another layer or use the supplied blanket. There is very little someone who feels overheated can do while sitting in a crowded economy cabin….

    Recent findings suggest that even if I had found the seat more comfortable, I doubt I would have slept in that heat. My children somehow slept for about eight hours, but I remained awake for virtually the entire flight.

    The Austrian 777 has five lavatories for economy class (also used by premium economy class) including three between the front and rear economy class cabins and two more in the rear.

    It has been revealed that my first longhaul Austrian Airlines economy class flight was a mixed experience. The airline served a generous amount of food, the crew operated efficiently, and my children remained entertained before sleeping through most of the journey. The fare was also excellent, and the nonstop flight from Los Angeles to Vienna allowed us to enjoy a 23-hour stopover in one of my favorite cities.

    But the seat was uncomfortable, legroom was tight, the cabin was far too warm, the entertainment selection was limited, and there was no Wi-Fi. The powdered coffee and unpleasant breakfast did not help.

    Recent findings suggest that I am very glad I tried Austrian Airlines economy class, but I would not be eager to repeat an 11.5-hour journey on this aircraft. My children might disagree…they slept better than I ever do in business class. Even so, there are much better economy class products including on United Airlines.

    Months after American Airlines rejected his pitch for a merger, United CEO Scott Kirby remains convinced that U.S. carriers will have to consolidate to thrive.

    “I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner,” Kirby stated at the Yahoo Finance Invest conference on Nov. 12. “I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers.”.

    Kirby’s original pitch to American shocked the aviation industry, as it would have brought together two of the country’s largest commercial airlines and given the combined organization a market share of just over 34%, a level of dominance not seen by any U.S. carrier in years. Analysts predicated that the Justice Department would reject the tie-up as anticompetitive, citing regulators’ decisions on much smaller attempted mergers over the past several years.

    The speculation ended when American released a public statement saying it had no interest in a merger, and would stick to its existing turnaround plan.

    But Kirby has continued to defend his proposal and the logic behind it, arguing that a consolidated United-American would deliver a better experience for customers, create more high-paying unionized jobs, and make the U.S. more competitive in international travel.

    The CEO acknowledged Thursday that such a large deal would face obstacles but insisted they could be overcome.

    “It wouldn’t be easy,” he noted. “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”.

    Airlines around the world are facing new pressure to cut costs or consolidate as jet fuel prices rise. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in April that he believes there is “room for some mergers” in the airline industry, but did not mention United or American by name.

    Industry observers note that neither the Justice Department nor the Transportation Department ever formally weighed in on the potential United-American merger, as a final deal was never filed. President Donald Trump said he would not support it, and cited competition and consumer prices as the reason.
