    Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
    • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
    • Industry observers note that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

    The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

    Industry observers note that “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s crucial that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

    While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

    Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

    The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

    “This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

    Sources indicate that “Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

    The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

    According to recent reports, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

    But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

    According to recent reports, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., noted voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

    “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

    Industry observers note that whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

    It has been revealed that “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they remarked, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

    According to recent reports, sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

    Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. John Kennedy, R-La., mentioned on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

    Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

    It has been revealed that sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

    Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides stated.

    It has been revealed that “It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

    That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

    Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

    “Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

    Industry observers note that “If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that air India has eliminated fuel stops in Rome on its flights from Delhi and Mumbai to Upcoming York, cutting some journeys by five hours.
    • Air India has restored nonstop service on all four of its routes linking Delhi and Mumbai with Fresh York JFK and Newark.
    • Flights that had taken approximately 22 hours with a technical stop in Rome are once again operating in about 17 hours.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that air India has eliminated fuel stops in Rome on its flights from Delhi and Mumbai to Upcoming York, cutting some journeys by five hours. The surprising key to restoring nonstop service was not Russian airspace, but the reopening of a shorter corridor over Iraq.

    Air India has restored nonstop service on all four of its routes linking Delhi and Mumbai with Fresh York JFK and Newark.

    Flights that had taken approximately 22 hours with a technical stop in Rome are once again operating in about 17 hours.

    Recent findings suggest that the Delhi flights are operated with Airbus A350-900 aircraft featuring business class suites, premium economy, and economy class. The Mumbai routes use refurbished Boeing 777-300ERs with first class, business class, premium economy, and economy class.

    Removing five hours from an already very long journey represents the difference between a difficult nonstop flight and a 22-hour saga involving an annoying fuel stop.

    Pakistan closed its airspace to Indian-operated aircraft, eliminating the most direct westbound corridor from India toward Europe and North America.

    Industry observers note that the conflict involving Iran then created further restrictions across the Middle East. Air India was forced to operate a much longer route through Jordan and Egypt before continuing across Europe and the Atlantic. That routing pushed the limits of what the aircraft could operate with a commercially useful payload. Air India consequently added a technical stop in Rome to refuel before continuing to New York.

    Industry observers note that the reopening of Iraqi airspace changed the calculation. Air India can now fly a shorter route across Iraq and Turkey before continuing through Europe and across the Atlantic.

    Industry observers note that the airline says this has reduced total journey time by as much as five hours. Additionally, the shorter route will reduce fuel consumption by approximately 10% and also ease crew scheduling pressures associated with flight-duty limits. Considering the cost of operating a fully loaded Airbus A350 or Boeing 777 for several additional hours, this is a substantial operational improvement for Air India as well as a welcome one for passengers.

    Air India remains permitted to use Russian airspace and has done so on certain North American routes, particularly services connecting India with the West Coast of the United States.

    Sources indicate that that has given Air India an advantage over U.S. and European airlines that avoid or are prohibited from using Russian airspace. But it would be incorrect to assume that Air India routinely flies over Russia when traveling between India and New York.

    The available flight-tracking data suggests otherwise.

    Recorded routes displayed by FlightPaths.com for Delhi–JFK show no use of Russian airspace in its sample of 20 flights. Among seven recorded Mumbai–JFK flights, just one crossed Russia. The pattern is even clearer in the opposite direction. Russia did not appear in the displayed samples of 20 JFK–Delhi flights or 10 JFK–Mumbai flights.

    Recent findings suggest that (Those samples are not a comprehensive record of every Air India flight, and routings can change based on winds, restrictions, and operational requirements. But they demonstrate that Russian airspace is not the normal solution for Air India’s Fresh York service).

    These flights generally travel westward through the Middle East and Europe, which why access to Iraqi airspace has such a large effect.

    Air India has restored nonstop flights from Delhi and Mumbai to Latest York JFK and Newark, cutting journey times by as much as five hours.

    The change was made possible by renewed access to Iraqi airspace, not by shifting these flights over Russia. Although Air India uses Russian airspace on some routes, flight-tracking data indicates that it is not routinely used for New York service.

    It has been revealed that A 17-hour flight remains very long, but it is much better than a 22-hour journey with an unwanted fuel stop in Rome. For passengers traveling between India and the Newly introduced York area, this is a genuine and substantial improvement…and ironically might allow Air India to charge a higher premium for its nonstop service, despite the fuel and labor savings this shorter flight time will produce.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that friday’s mass grounding could cost the four largest U.S.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that friday’s mass grounding could cost the four largest U.S. airlines a combined $345 million or more, according to investment firm Bernstein.

    The estimate, first reported by Reuters, comes after more than 18,000 flights were canceled on Friday and over the weekend, upending travel aims for hundreds of thousands of people both in and outside the U.S.

    According to recent reports, bernstein’s projection includes lost earnings at United, Delta, American Airlines, and Southwest. The financial hit for other U.S. carriers, such as JetBlue, Alaska Airlines, and Frontier, could push the total impact to over half a billion dollars.

    More exact information about potential losses will come with the airlines’ fourth-quarter earnings reports.

    Flight disruptions eased somewhat Monday, and the FAA expects air traffic to normalize by the evening. But questions remain about the cause of Friday’s ATC outage, and it could take days, weeks, or even longer to get a clear picture of exactly what went wrong.

    U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy remarked Saturday that a router installed by contractor L3Harris as part of a routine copper line-to-fiber optic upgrade “flooded” other routers with data, causing the crash. It was not clear if L3Harris incorrectly installed the router, or if the device itself was faulty, Duffy said.

    That explanation has drawn some pushback, most notably from Hewlett Packard, the parent company of Juniper Networks, which makes the routers L3Harris was installing. HP noted the Juniper device was “functioning exactly as intended” based on available information.

    Additionally, some anonymous air traffic controllers have charged that the secretary’s narrative does not match with what they saw unfold in towers and control rooms during the ground stop.

    L3Harris stated Saturday that it is working with the FAA to determine why the outage occurred.

    Guide: United Airlines Has Starlink On More Than Half Its Flights, But These Aircraft Offer The Best Odds

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines has reached an impressive milestone: Starlink is now available on more than half of its daily flights.
    • United confirmed last week that Starlink had crossed the 50% threshold across its daily schedule.
    • That is an extraordinarily fast rollout for an airline with more than 1,000 mainline aircraft plus a large regional fleet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines has reached an impressive milestone: Starlink is now available on more than half of its daily flights. I increasingly choose United when I know Starlink will be onboard, but customers generally cannot determine that when booking. Here is what United should change and which aircraft currently offer your best chance of getting Starlink.

    United confirmed last week that Starlink had crossed the 50% threshold across its daily schedule. The airline expects that number to approach 64% by the end of 2026 and aims to complete fleetwide installations by the end of 2027.

    That is an extraordinarily fast rollout for an airline with more than 1,000 mainline aircraft plus a large regional fleet.

    Industry observers note that the announcement was packaged around Thanksgiving travel, with United expecting to carry more than 6.6 million passengers between November 19 and December 1. But the more consequential development is that Starlink is no longer a novelty you might encounter on a regional jet. Instead, it is becoming a defining part of the United experience.

    I have used just about every major inflight internet system, and Starlink is clearly the best.

    Recent findings suggest that the connection is fast, latency is low, and it works well enough that I can complete almost everything onboard that I would ordinarily do from my office. Large files load quickly, video calls are possible (but thankfully not allowed on United), and the service supports multiple devices. It is also free for MileagePlus members.

    That changes how I value a flight.

    If two departures are similarly priced and one has Starlink, I will choose the Starlink flight. I may even accept a slightly less convenient departure time because several productive hours in the air are worth far more to me than leaving an hour earlier.

    That is precisely the sort of customer behavior United wants. Scott Kirby has repeatedly suggested that Starlink will persuade customers loyal to other airlines to try United, after which the rest of the experience will convince them to stay.

    I understand his confidence. Once you experience internet that works almost like it does on the ground, returning to a slow or unreliable connection is painful.

    Here is the problem: United generally does not confirm Starlink availability until three days before departure.

    According to recent reports, the airline offers a useful Starlink tracker, but it is designed to check an upcoming flight rather than help someone choose among flights several weeks or months in advance. By the time the tracker confirms the aircraft, most passengers have already purchased their tickets.

    Aircraft substitutions will always occur, and no airline can guarantee that a particular tail number will operate a flight. But that does not prevent United from displaying the expected connectivity during booking.

    It has been revealed that united already identifies many onboard features in the reservation process. It could add a Starlink indicator based on the scheduled aircraft, accompanied by a clear disclaimer that equipment may change. Even an imperfect forecast would be useful.

    Recent findings suggest that united carefully claims Starlink is available on more than half of its daily flights, which is not the same as saying more than half of its aircraft or passenger seats have Starlink. Regional jets and narrowbody aircraft generally operate more flights per day than widebody aircraft, allowing each installation to influence a larger number of departures.

    Recent findings suggest that united’s entire two-cabin regional fleet now has Starlink. If you want the best chance of getting it, book a flight operated by a Bombardier CRJ-550 or Embraer E175.

    If you are traveling on a mainline aircraft, the Airbus A321neo is most likely to have Starlink, with 88% of that fleet equipped. The Boeing 737-800 follows at 77%, while 67% of the Boeing 737-900 fleet has it.

    In a recent development, avoid the Airbus A319, Airbus A320, and Boeing 757-300 if connectivity is crucial to you. None right now have Starlink, and the aging Panasonic systems installed on some of those aircraft are most likely not to work at all.

    Recent findings suggest that personally, I avoid 757-300s and go out of my way to fly on A321neos. You should too if onboard connectivity is crucial to you.

    Progress on the widebody fleet remains slow. Only 2% of United’s Boeing 787 fleet and 5% of its Boeing 777 fleet currently have Starlink, while none of its Boeing 767s are equipped.

    Delta Air Lines has selected Amazon Leo for its next-generation internet, with installations scheduled to begin in 2028. As I discussed yesterday, a rocket failure that destroyed 40 Amazon satellites illustrates the risk of selecting a network that is still being constructed.

    In a recent development, delta already offers free Wi-Fi on most of its fleet, and I have found it perfectly usable on many flights. This is not a choice between internet and no internet. But in terms of functionality, Starlink is better. It is not even a contest.

    United may complete its fleetwide rollout before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft. That gives United time to turn a technical advantage into a behavioral one: customers try Starlink, discover they can be more productive in the air, and begin considering connectivity when selecting future flights.

    That is why displaying Starlink during booking would be valuable. If the product is strong enough to influence purchasing decisions, United should make it easier for customers to find before purchasing.

    Industry observers note that it would also help reduce disappointments. I was recently on a Boeing 777-200 with old-school Panasonic Wi-Fi, and a business class passenger across the aisle from me was fuming that there was no Starlink. Better to underpromise and overdeliver than the other way around.

    Recent findings suggest that starlink is now available on more than half of United Airlines flights and should reach nearly 64% by the end of the year. That is impressive progress and gives United a genuine advantage over its domestic competitors.

    Sources indicate that I increasingly choose flights based on whether Starlink will be onboard. The frustration is that United generally cannot confirm it until three days before departure, long after the booking decision has been made.

    A Starlink indicator during booking would not need to be a guarantee. It could simply tell customers what United reasonably expects to offer. In the meantime, regional jets, Airbus A321neos, and Boeing 737-800s give you the best shot at Starlink on United.

    Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
    • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
    • Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

    Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

    Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

    Sources indicate that sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the latest year.

    It has been revealed that “Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

    The nomination of Thumann Severs, who presently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

    Presently Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

    Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

    According to recent reports, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., said Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

    “A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper stated.

    In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

    Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

    Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC right now focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

    Sources indicate that committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he mentioned Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

    Sources indicate that “The First Amendment places important limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz said. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

    Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

    According to recent reports, however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

    “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she remarked. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

    Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs remarked she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

    Industry observers note that luján also asked Thumann Severs to name concerns where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she noted her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

    In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

    According to recent reports, thumann Severs stated that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

    Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

    According to recent reports, “Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any latest Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

    On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

    “Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

    Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been announced by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century.
    • What has changed since then is the crowds.
    • Whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, amsterdam today looks remarkably similar to how it did on my first visit as a high schooler over a decade ago, with its maze of canals, steady flow of bikes, and gabled façades—many of which have stood there since the 17th century. To a history-loving teenager visiting Europe for the first time, the Dutch capital was a wonderland of Van Goghs. It felt so different from my hometown, yet still approachable, and sparked my lifelong love of travel.

    What has changed since then is the crowds. Amsterdam is now one of Europe's most visited cities, so you'll need to book tickets to the major sites well in advance, especially during summer. The same goes for accommodations. On more than a dozen return trips (many by train from Belgium, where I used to live), I have stayed everywhere from youth hostels to boutique hotels to Airbnbs. And over the years, I've learned that renting an Airbnb offers a completely different way to experience the city.

    Whether you're looking for a classic canal house in the Jordaan, a design-forward houseboat along the Amstel, or a multi-level family home near Vondelpark, the rentals on this list can help you settle into the city in your own way. Read on for a few of my favorite Airbnbs in Amsterdam, whether you're here for the art, the nightlife, or to explore by bike.

    We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

    Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, separate kitchen, quiet street.

    According to recent reports, couples or small families who want to stay in the heart of old Amsterdam will adore this renovated one-bedroom inside a historic canal house on one of the city's widest canals. The roughly 650-square-foot space sleeps up to three, and the separate kitchen has a large dining table. Step outside and you're around the corner from lively Nieuwmarkt, where cafés line the market square. Or, check out the dim sum spots in nearby Chinatown. Despite the proximity to so much activity, previous guests say the street itself stays peaceful at night. Just be prepared to haul your luggage up a steep staircase, as is expected for most Amsterdam buildings.

    Neighborhood: Centrum (Nieuwmarkt)Things to do nearby: Rembrandt House Museum, De Oude Kerk.

    Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private garden, dedicated playroom, fireplace.

    As in most major European cities, space is at a premium in Amsterdam, which makes this industrial-style town house a real find for families. It even has a dedicated playroom packed with toys and books. It sits in Oud-West, a grid-like neighborhood just outside the central canal ring, steps from the daily Ten Kate Market. When the weather cooperates, fire up the Weber grill in the private garden out back. Inside, a gas fireplace warms the light-filled living room and kitchen. But you may not find yourself cooking much, since the home's location puts you right near the Foodhallen. Three bedrooms sleep up to four, with a king bed, a double bed, and a toddler bed.

    Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Foodhallen, Ten Kate Market, Vondelpark.

    Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Heated pool, private garden, Nintendo Wii.

    Groups who want to dip in and out of city life should take a look at this detached four-bedroom house in a tranquil, residential corner of Amsterdam Noord. The nearby metro reaches Central Station in about five minutes (or you can bike there in 15), and the countryside is close by too. The highlight, however, is the large private garden, where you'll find a heated pool (open roughly April through October) and a sauna. There's also a grill and space to dine outdoors. During the colder months, your crew will probably prefer curling up on the cozy couch for a movie or a round of games on the Nintendo Wii. Practical perks include a washer and dryer, a dedicated workspace, and four bedrooms.

    Neighborhood: Amsterdam NoordThings to do nearby: Eye Filmmuseum, A'DAM Lookout, NDSM Wharf.

    In a recent development, if your image of the perfect trip to Amsterdam includes staying in an authentic canal house, then consider this character-filled apartment in the leafy Jordaan neighborhood. Guests enter through the roomy breakfast area on the ground floor, and upstairs, you'll find a living area filled with plush furniture, jewel-toned accents, and views of the canal, Anne Frank House, and Westerkerk (Western Church). There's one true bedroom with a king bed and a pull-out couch in the living room. The hosts, who warmly welcome families with little ones, provide lots of kid-friendly necessities, like a high chair.

Gather in the dining area (there's also a full kitchen) or around the fireplace in the cozy living room stocked with board games, a vinyl collection, and even a piano. Stained-glass windows and art-covered walls are fitting for the prime location near the Rijksmuseum and Van Gogh Museum. However, be prepared to carry your luggage up some steep and narrow steps.

    Neighborhood: VondelparkThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum.

    Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Air-conditioning, sparkling water on tap, large garden patio.

    According to recent reports, this spacious luxury apartment in a historic building offers some perks that can be hard to come by in Amsterdam: air-conditioning (in the living room and one bedroom), no stairs to climb, sparkling water on tap, and a living room that opens onto a garden patio with a lovely view of the Rijksmuseum. Families with small kids can also request a travel crib, high chair, and other gear. Plus, there isn't much for little hands to grab onto thanks to the minimalist decor. The two bedrooms each feature plush king beds.

    Neighborhood: MuseumpleinThings to do nearby: Stedelijk Museum, Van Gogh Museum, Rijksmuseum.

    Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fitness equipment, chef's kitchen, dedicated workspace with printer.

    According to recent reports, want to feel really at home for an extended stay? Save this open-strategy loft housed inside a converted 19th-century police station, which stands out with a dedicated workspace (desk, monitor, printer) and fitness equipment (kettlebells, dumbbells, rowing machine). There's also a chef's kitchen and an Art Deco–style bathroom. French doors open up onto a back terrace, and huge bay windows offer a view of a 17th-century church and the Noordermarkt, where an open-air market sets up shop twice a week.

    Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Noordermarkt, Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets.

    Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sage espresso machine, speakers and sound system, easy tram access.

    According to recent reports, this bright one-bedroom in Oud-West sits just outside the central canal ring and combines high ceilings and ornate moldings with a modern, open kitchen and sunlit living space. Double doors lead to a quiet queen bedroom with a larger balcony in the back. A smaller front balcony overlooks the street, where a tram stops just outside and connects guests with the rest of the city. Guests will also find a supermarket right across the street and restaurants and cafés around the corner.

    Neighborhood: Oud-WestThings to do nearby: Vondelpark, Foodhallen, De Filmhallen.

    Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Waterfront views, indoor fireplace, washer and dryer.

    It has been revealed that think you have to choose between space and character in an Airbnb? Think again. This sleek, 2,600-square-foot houseboat on the Amstel River—yes, the river that gave Amsterdam its name—offers one bedroom, one-and-a-half baths, a full kitchen, and three terraces. In summer, watch boats drift by or take out the provided paddleboards—then cool off inside in the air-conditioning. After winter rolls in, curl up by the suspended fireplace as you gaze out of the floor-to-ceiling windows.

    Neighborhood: De PijpThings to do nearby: Heineken Experience, Albert Cuyp Market, Sarphatipark.

    Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Room-darkening shades, television with Chromecast and Netflix, access to outdoor patio.

    According to recent reports, it may be on a quiet street, but this compact studio puts you close to the action, with Central Station just a couple of minutes' walk away. Light floods in through the three large windows with canal views, and the orange and copper-colored accents create a warm and inviting vibe. There's also access to a private rooftop terrace if you need a bit of fresh air. Be prepared to carry your luggage up a tricky flight of steep and narrow stairs in this fairly typical Amsterdam building that dates back to 1790.

    Neighborhood: CentrumThings to do nearby: Dam Square, De Oude Kerk.

    Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canalside location, television with Netflix, washer and dryer.

    Stay right on the famous Keizersgracht (Emperor's Canal) in this first-floor apartment equipped with a washer and dryer and a full kitchen with a stove, fridge, and sink. Large, front-facing windows flood the crisp white apartment with natural light and offer a front-row seat to the city life buzzing by outside. It's also just around the corner from the Anne Frank House. The bedroom features a king-size bed, ideal for relaxing after a long day of exploring.

    Neighborhood: Grachtengordel (Canal ring)Things to do nearby: Anne Frank House, The 9 Streets, Dam Square.

    Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Canal view, garden access, host's personal art collection.

    Laid-back solo travelers or couples will appreciate this homey rental located on a quiet street near a few museums within walking distance of the lively Leidseplein Square. It’s wonderful for those looking to take a step back from the hustle and bustle—not the best pick for all-night partiers. The living space blends modern and vintage flourishes, featuring French paintings that are part of the owner's personal art collection and front windows overlooking a canal. A floor-to-ceiling window in the back opens to a lovely shared garden with outdoor seating where you can have coffee or tea on warm mornings.

    Neighborhood: JordaanThings to do nearby: Leidseplein, Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum.

    What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Amsterdam?

    It has been revealed that book a stay in the Grachtengordel (canal ring) for the quintessential Amsterdam experience. The Jordaan has a similarly atmospheric feel with slightly quieter surroundings, while the Museum District puts the city's famous art museums right at your doorstep.

    When is the best season to visit Amsterdam?

    Recent findings suggest that spring is one of the best times to visit. It's when the city wakes up from the long winter and the Netherlands's colorful tulips burst into bloom (plan a day trip to the famous Keukenhof Gardens, about 40 minutes away). Come for King's Day on April 27, when the entire city turns bright orange with street parties and canal boat parades, or visit on the brink of summertime, in late May or June, and you'll enjoy much longer days, with daylight sometimes lasting past 9 p.m.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet.
    • Lufthansa has opened bookings for its new “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.
    • It has been revealed that each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet. The newly introduced seats will cost extra, even for passengers already booked in business class, but I welcome the option. After years of selling an economy seat with a blocked middle as business class, this is an upgrade worth getting excited about. It is a welcome change for an airline more accustomed to following competitors than setting the standard.

    Lufthansa has opened bookings for its new “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.

    It has been revealed that each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2. Features include:.

    The six aircraft will also receive Starlink Wi-Fi during the retrofit.

    These are recliners rather than flat beds, but they will represent a substantial improvement over the standard European business class seat, particularly on longer flights, which for those unaware is simply a regular economy class seat with the adjacent seat blocked.

    The first modified aircraft is scheduled to enter service on December 16, 2026, initially operating various routes.

    Dedicated deployment begins in February 2027, with seat reservations now available for flights from March 1, 2027:.

    Look for the Premium Business Seat designation when booking:.

    Notice all three routes are leisure?

    Lufthansa is retaining its standard business class offering behind the recliners. Business class passengers can select the larger seat during booking or subsequently through seat reservations, subject to the buy-up price: buying business class will not automatically get you a business class recliner on these routes.

    I can already hear the objections: passengers are paying a premium for business class and then being asked to pay again for a better seat. But this is quite different than what intra-Europe business class has been for as long as I can remember on Lufthansa (except for the old A300s) and I would still rather have this option than continue with the blocked-middle arrangement as the only choice.

    Lufthansa calls this a “commercial test.” Demand and the response to its booking options will determine whether the concept expands, but I think this concept is going to do great.

    Recent findings suggest that I wrote about the Eurowings Premium BIZ concept when it was announced last year. It was rather amusing that the budget carrier would introduce proper narrowbody business class seating before its “full service” Lufthansa Group siblings.

    Industry observers note that that project was intended to test the concept for other airlines within the group. Now we are seeing a similar approach at Lufthansa itself. The conventional European model has an operational advantage: airlines can move the curtain to adjust the size of business class. Dedicated recliners make that space less flexible.

    Installing a small permanent cabin while retaining conventional business class behind it strikes me as a reasonable compromise. Lufthansa can sell the larger seats to passengers willing to pay for them and still expand the rest of business class when demand warrants. I would particularly like to see this spread to longer routes across the group. An empty middle seat is welcome, but it becomes a rather thin comfort proposition when you are spending several hours onboard, especially with those uncomfortable Recaro slimline seats.

    Recent findings suggest that one Mile At A Time suggests that Air France should introduce proper business class seats throughout its Airbus A220 fleet. I love that idea…SWISS should do the same.

    The A220 offers an especially compelling opportunity because its economy cabin is arranged 2-3. With adjacent seats blocked in business class, Air France sells only three seats per row.

    Sources indicate that A proper 2-2 business class cabin would allow it to sell four seats across while giving passengers a wider seat. Additional legroom would consume more cabin length, of course, so the calculation is not quite as simple as adding another paying passenger in every existing row, but I think the math would work.

    For illustration, replacing three conventional business class rows with two recliner rows would reduce capacity from nine passengers to eight. That is a modest reduction in exchange for a much better product, though the actual economics would depend on the seat dimensions and final layout.

    I have already experienced what this could look like on my Bulgaria Air A220-300 flight from Sofia to Amsterdam. The airline offered proper recliners in a 2-2 layout, with leg rests and power outlets. I found it an excellent way to spend three hours flying within Europe.

    Air France and SWISS have invested heavily in its premium reputation. A small recliner cabin on the A220 would extend that investment to the European flights that often begin or end a longhaul business class journey.

    We do not need a flat bed from Paris to Amsterdam or Zurich to London, but on longer European routes, a comfortable recliner would give me another reason to choose one carrier over another.

    Lufthansa will install eight Premium Business Seats on each of six Airbus A320s, with bookings now open for select Frankfurt flights to Athens, Nice, and Cairo from March 2027.

    The surcharge will bother some passengers, understandably, but I think it makes sense and am pleased to see Lufthansa offer a better seat and hope the test succeeds.

    Industry observers note that eurowings demonstrated a willingness to try something different. Lufthansa is following. Perhaps Air France, SWISS, and others will see an opportunity too. European business class has room to improve, and a seat that is actually different from economy is a very good place to start.

    According to recent reports, the first time I traveled with an aluminum suitcase, I emerged into the airport with a whole newly introduced energy.     But while the style is an undeniable draw, beyond the immediate hit of glamour, aluminum luggage offers some practical perks too. It offers greater structural protection than polycarbonate and soft-shell options—you can’t really argue with that, given it’s the type of material they make planes out of. And these durable suitcases are typically fitted with secure latch locking mechanisms over temperamental zippers, with steel corners and frames designed to comfortably absorb bumps, drops, and scrapes on the go.

    Investing in high-end aluminum luggage is a serious price commitment—especially when considering that there are plenty of excellent soft-sided and hard-shell suitcases on the market. It’s why putting these more expensive suitcases through their paces in real-world scenarios is essential for our testing.

Below, the select few of our editors’ favorite aluminum suitcase to travel with for every type of trip.

    What are the benefits of aluminum luggage?

    It has been revealed that aluminum luggage offers superior durability and protection compared to fabric or plastic alternatives. Its rigid, crush-proof shell and heavy-duty frame safeguard fragile contents against rough handling and impact during transit. Aluminum suitcases come finished with latches instead of vulnerable zippers, creating an airtight, water-resistant seal that deters theft. Aluminum is built to last a lifetime, developing a distinctive, travel-worn patina over time rather than tearing or cracking. Then there’s that effortlessly sleek aesthetic at the airport, which is another fun perk.

    How we tested the best aluminum luggage:.

    Our editors have personally tested a wide range of bags from leading luggage brands, carefully selecting their favorites based on function, innovation, and design. Each suitcase was thoroughly tested in-office by our editors before being taken on trips by members of the wider team for real-world use. During testing, we assess overall build quality, wheel performance, TSA-approved locks, design features such as external pockets and laptop compartments, and overall value. Weight, size, usability, and visual appeal are also carefully considered.

    Tech Report: Inside the 2026 Condé Nast Traveler Points of View Summit

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, on November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in Upcoming York City for a day exploring the latest in travel.
    • In a recent development, global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on major-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences.
    • Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, on November 12, our ninth annual Points of View Summit brought together trip designers, luxury planners, and on-the-ground experts in Upcoming York City for a day exploring the latest in travel. While unrelenting rain poured outside, the atmosphere inside was anything but dreary and gray.

    In a recent development, global editorial director Divia Thani kicked things off with opening remarks on major-picture trends: how American travelers are driving luxury travel; the transfer of wealth to a younger generation; and a shift from spending on products to lived experiences. These overarching themes gave the audience a preview of what would come later in the day on panels and in breakout sessions. From a talk about Hilton Head’s Gullah culture and a run-through of reasons to visit Morocco—yes, this bit was accompanied by a post-lunch tea ceremony—to an exchange on all-inclusives with Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and a sit-down unpacking food and memory with Antoni Porowski, the day was full of thoughtful exchanges that reminded us why we journey in the first place. After much applause, the summit concluded with a cocktail party featuring wines from San Miguel de Allende and a taste of Lowcountry South Carolina by way of shrimp, grits, and fried green tomatoes—there was lots to celebrate, with a decade of Hilton Head being on our Readers' Choice Awards and its Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport drawing visitors from all over. Below, explore all that went down at our 2026 Points of View Summit.

    Our editors discuss next year's editorial coverage themes, including spotlight destinations and how we're tapping into pop culture.

    Industry observers note that the day kicked off with a roundtable over what’s been on our minds and what'll be on our editorial calendar next year, just in time for our 40th anniversary. Our features director Rebecca Misner led the conversation with Thani, global features director Erin Florio, global executive director of video Dana Kravis, senior features editor Megan Spurrell, and associate editor Charlie Hobbs, who all agreed that a demand for substantive, long-form storytelling is back (though did it ever truly leave?). Spurrell shared an early preview of the now-live Best Places to Go in 2027, including destinations like the Albanian Alps for hiking, Memphis for museum openings, Yunnan for a slew of newly introduced restaurants, and more. Kravis spoke about cross-platform stories such as our new video series Made In, exploring craft in a particular destination, and upcoming video iterations of series like On Location, which unpacks beloved film and show locations. On the topic of pop culture, Hobbs highlighted a continued focus on cultural happenings, sporting events, and festivals that we're keeping on our radar as reasons to travel. Ultimately, going into 2027, Florio mentioned, our coverage will explore “what it is that drives us to travel, as opposed to where it is we want to go"—not only the destination for destination's sake, but the experiences and impulses underlying travelers' choices.

    Eduardo Schutte and Madison Flager discuss the future of the all-inclusive stay and Hyatt's rapidly growing portfolio.

    Next up, commerce director Madison Flager spoke with Eduardo Schutte, Hyatt Inclusive Collection’s commercial SVP, on how all-inclusive stays have evolved and expanded far beyond your typical beachside bubbles to meet globetrotters of all kinds. In an age of optimization, it's only natural that travelers would value the ease and confidence of a bundled vacation, with less time spent planning so that they can enjoy their destination sans stress. Schutte observed that Hyatt Inclusive Collection has grown from two properties in 2013 to over 120 today, with expansion well underway in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia. “You're going to know exactly how much your vacation is, so it's much more predictable and easier to initiative,” Schutte remarked. Afterwards, one lucky guest won a trip to a Hyatt Inclusive Resort. Perhaps the all-inclusive is a remedy for the times.

    Erin Florio helms the conversation on summer travel, from increasing shoulder season trips to less crowded destinations.

    We recently unpacked why it seems everyone took a fallcation this year, and spotlighted the year-round appeal of off-season Greece. Though the once-sweltering days of the summer months might be all you’re yearning for as winter fast approaches, increasingly unpredictable weather and overcrowded destinations are shifting and expanding the typical high season. Florio led this panel with Jack Ezon, founder and managing partner of Embark Beyond; Catherine Heald, CEO and founder of Remote Lands; Jade McBride, president of Ted Turner Reserves; Scott Jordan, vice president of sales–East at Delta Air Lines; and Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina.

    Industry observers note that to Ezon, it's less about the timing and more about the value of a trip; entry-level Mediterranean rooms can cost $4,000 to $6,000 per night, raising questions about whether the experience delivers value beyond price. Reframing a destination’s appeal beyond one season is key—going to Amalfi in October for wine or December for Christmas markets—as per Jordan, who stressed the value of meeting travelers where they're headed. He noted Delta is extending and adding seasonal service, including earlier flights to Porto and routes to Copenhagen, Sardinia, and Prague. Still, the group wondered whether greater access to Sardinia might relieve pressure on Amalfi and Como or simply congest another destination.

    It has been revealed that zhang said her clients aren't choosing between European hotspots at all; they're set on Asia, the choice becoming whether to visit Japan or China. In 2025, China saw sweeping growth in international visitors, which Zhang credited to new visa policies, renewed country perceptions, and a global interest in regional lifestyles. “I just think that's part of wellness. It's drinking hot water, wearing slippers, playing mahjong, being social with family," she said. "A lot of these concepts are promoting China as a way of living, rather than as a destination.”.

    Katie Mathews and Omolola Campbell on Hilton Head Island's Gullah culture.

    In a recent development, for a chat presented by Hilton Head Island, senior creative producer Katie Mathews sat down with Omolola Campbell, executive producer of The Spirit We Move With, a short documentary about South Carolina's Gullah community. The Gullah people are the descendants of West Africans who were brought to the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida, in the 1700s and 1800s for slavery. A sixth-gen Gullah descendant herself, Campbell spoke with Mathews on the importance of leading the narrative and memorializing these stories today. In South Carolina’s case, it’s about hearing from Gullah people themselves. Campbell uses her gift shop on the island, Binya, as a space for educating customers through handwoven sweetgrass baskets, cookbooks, prints, and more. “People say that storytelling is a way of preservation. I like to say conservation, because to preserve something is to put it on a shelf, [but] Gullah culture is still alive and thriving,” Campbell said.

    In between panels, Mei Zhang and others tried Moroccan tea.

    In a recent development, hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi discuss lesser-known Moroccan cities and itineraries.

    According to recent reports, after breakout sessions with editors and travel specialists, guests were served Moroccan tea before settling into a chat with news editor Hannah Towey and Ms. Siham Fettouhi, North America executive director of the Moroccan National Tourism Office. Beyond Marrakech and the desert, Fettouhi noted the country's appeal lies in its Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines and can't-miss surfing spots. "We're talking about a country that offers you the possibility to ski literally in the morning and enjoy sunset in the beach in the afternoon," Fettouhi noted. “Morocco has never been this accessible from North America," she continued, mentioning nonstop flights now available from North America through Royal Air Maroc, Air Canada, Air Transat, Delta, and United. And domestic travel is also getting an update, as Morocco's high-speed rail network, Al Boraq, has extensions planned toward Marrakech and Agadir ahead of the 2030 World Cup.

    An attendee captures Lale Arikoglu and Antoni Porowski's culinary conversation.

    Recent findings suggest that we closed out Points of View with a chat between Lale Arikoglu, director of special projects, and Antoni Porowski, Emmy-winning producer, Queer Eye veteran, and host of National Geographic's Best of the World series, which aired in June. While his other Nat Geo series No Taste Like Home traces family histories through food, this more recent show highlights the people behind well-known destinations' institutions and traditions—think a mustachioed clockmaker at Substantial Ben's Great Clock or a family-run cheese cave in Paris. “There’s always a beautiful nerd that’s behind this larger-than-life thing that millions of us have had a chance to experience,” Porowski noted with a laugh, referencing folks not unlike himself, dedicated to that one experience and sharing it with others.

    In a recent development, for Porowski, it's food that has offered a way to connect people with their roots and family histories, inspired in large part by his own journey toward embracing his Polish heritage. While planning a retirement trip for his dad several years ago, Porowski stated his dad insisted they visit the Polish mountain village Zakopane. “We tried soups that I hadn't had since I was six or seven years old and got to connect through that,” he recalled. Porowski wrapped up the conversation with a handful of anecdotes from filming No Taste Like Home; a particular favorite was being in Senegal with Issa Rae, where he learned about teraanga, or the concept of generosity and sharing so integral to the West African country. Plus, the conversation would not have been complete without a rapid-fire round—see Porowski's answers below.

    Delta does Shake Shack, which I’m not opposed to. I would say nine times out of 10—unless I’m sleeping and it's a red-eye—I’ll always have it, even if the chicken’s rubbery.

    When the drinks cart goes by, what’s your go-to?

    Chamomile tea, typically. This is so random, but it’s something I had as a child: sparkling water with a splash of apple juice. It feels really chic.

    In a recent development, because my parents taught me to arrive for a flight 10 minutes before it takes off when we lived in West Virginia, Jaeger Airport in Charleston, West Virginia. You can show up like 30 minutes before with checked luggage, and they will let you on.

    Recent findings suggest that aisle, because I get to look at the flight attendants and see if they’re nervous during turbulence. But if they’re not, I know I’m fine.

    There’s nothing more powerful than grabbing your carry-on.

    Tomato bisque with a patty melt on sourdough focaccia from Il Buco Alimentari with sharp Vermont clothbound cheddar. That would be my appetizer, then puntarelle as my salad dish. For a main course, the shrimp from ABC Cocina—they have a lovely chili oil with lime zest and pink peppercorns—with again more bread to sop up all those oils. Since it’s my last meal, we’re doing surf and turf, scalloped potatoes, and a little broccoli rabe for fiber—no, I don’t care about fiber. For dessert, I was thinking about Campo de’ Fiori’s wild strawberries, with whipped cream and crème brûlée. I would finish it off with that Moroccan tea.

    Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E.
    • Recent findings suggest that but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens.
    • Sources indicate that “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

    Recent findings suggest that but Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete strategy” that provides change.

    Sources indicate that “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

    Sanders stated during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a newly introduced and bold direction.”.

    “I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

    According to recent reports, “Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

    Recent findings suggest that some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

    A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking remarked he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

    Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

    Sources indicate that “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete initiative that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

    She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

    Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen mentioned, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

    “What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”.

    Sources indicate that van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he mentioned, according to a livestream of the event.

    Industry observers note that schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

    Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

    Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

    Recent findings suggest that “That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

    Industry observers note that gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is at the moment leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

    Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

    Industry observers note that sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to proposal together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., stated Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Yes,” he remarked of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

    “And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

    Trump Blames Buttigieg For FAA Meltdown While Elon Musk Blames Sean Duffy

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown.
    • Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:.
    • When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown. Elon Musk, meanwhile, is pointing at the tTransportation Secretary Trump appointed, claiming Sean Duffy rejected an offer of free Starlink service. The finger-pointing continues, but neither accusation tells stranded passengers exactly why a router installation brought the system down.

    Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:.

    “Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.”.

    When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:.

    “I don’t take any responsibility.”.

    He also praised Duffy and attributed the disruption to aging equipment. I have already addressed the problem with blaming the previous administration. America’s air traffic control infrastructure has suffered from decades of deferred investment. That includes the Biden administration, but also Trump’s first term and the administrations before it.

    Sources indicate that friday’s failure, however, occurred during work performed under the current administration. An explanation of what Buttigieg allegedly did wrong would be useful, but of course Buttigieg is just the whipping boy for an administration that reveals no personal responsibly for any of its deleterious actions.

    According to recent reports, musk has offered a different accusation. In a post on X, he wrote:.

    Recent findings suggest that “Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he noted they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.”.

    It has been revealed that free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he mentioned they were not needed. As it turns out, they were. https://t.co/OZwDeiXOAr.

    — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026.

    That is a pointed criticism of the same official Trump indicates handled the situation well, but Musk does not explain when the offer was made, what equipment or service was included, where it would have been deployed, or how it would have prevented this particular failure…what a surprise.

    I would like Duffy to answer the allegation directly. Was there an offer? What did it cover? Why was it declined? If the proposal was unsuitable, explain why.

    Sources indicate that musk should also substantiate his assertion that the service would have been needed here. Being able to offer satellite internet does not establish that his proposed “gift” would have kept this particular network operating.

    Industry observers note that I love Starlink as an airline passenger. It is easily the best inflight internet service available now, and it increasingly influences which flights I book. But that does not mean it is or would have been a solution to an air traffic control network failure.

    It has been revealed that according to the FAA’s explanation, excessive connection attempts flooded its telecommunications network, destabilizing aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including installing a new router. Blocking those locations apparently stabilized the network. The broadcasting function on the new routers was also disabled as a precaution.

    To support Musk’s claim, we would need to know whether his proposed Starlink connections would have bypassed the affected equipment and preserved the necessary communications. Perhaps Starlink could have provided useful redundancy…but maybe the proposed installation would have had no bearing on this failure.

    Buttigieg has defended his record, pointing to improvements in controller staffing, runway safety, and flight cancellations during his tenure.

    He also says he rolled out the communications modernization project that the current administration is continuing. His response asks for an accounting of the money already authorized and an explanation of why the execution of that work triggered such a widespread failure.

    As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in… https://t.co/68KleIhFEc.

    — Pete Buttigieg (@PeteButtigieg) November 16, 2026.

    Industry observers note that they do not mean Buttigieg’s tenure should escape scrutiny. The January 2023 nationwide ground stop occurred on his watch, and the system still required enormous investment when he left office while his boss prioritized student loan forgiveness and federal mask mandates instead of accelerating infrastructure programs like Air Traffic Control modernization.

    But acknowledging those shortcomings does not relieve the current administration of responsibility for its own decisions. Duffy has been Transportation Secretary for nearly two years. He oversees the department responsible for explaining this failure and should be held accountable for the actions under his watch.

    There is an obvious temptation to enjoy the spectacle: Trump blames Buttigieg while Musk suggests Trump’s own transportation secretary rejected help. I find the contradiction revealing, but passengers deserve something more useful than competing accusations.

    It has been revealed that the investigation must establish what changed in the network, why that change caused such a widespread disruption, and whether the safeguards surrounding the work were adequate. Congress should examine the Starlink allegation too, if Musk can provide a concrete proposal and evidence supporting his account.

    According to recent reports, duffy may have had reasonable grounds to decline whatever Musk offered, but he should be able to articulate them. Likewise, Musk may have identified a missed opportunity, but he should be able to demonstrate his rather glaring accusation.

    Sources indicate that and Trump should stop treating an investigation as unnecessary because he has already identified a political opponent to blame. The age of the equipment was known. The difficult task was upgrading it while maintaining reliable service. That is the work his administration undertook, and that is the work it must explain to a weary public.

    Trump claims Buttigieg ruined the system and accepts no personal responsibility. Musk says Duffy rejected free Starlink service that was needed. Both claims deserve scrutiny and neither establishes the technical cause of Friday’s meltdown.

    According to recent reports, I would be far more receptive to an administration that acknowledged a failure during a difficult modernization project and explained how it would improve the process. Instead, we keep receiving accusations, praise for the response, and demands for more money.

    The passengers who lost days getting home deserve a candid explanation of what went wrong. So do the taxpayers being asked to fund the repair. Is this really a political issue that should divide us?
