    Condor Asks Passengers To Share Magazines To Save On Fuel Costs

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It’s obviously a tough time for many airlines around the globe, given the impact that higher jet fuel prices are having on economics, in an industry with razor thin margins.
    • It has been revealed that aeroTELEGRAPH flags how as of November 1, 2026, German airline Condor has slashed the number of inflight shopping magazines it has onboard flights.
    • Sources indicate that the airline has confirmed that the goal is “to reduce the weight on board and thus fuel consumption,” and it’s pointed out how the inflight shopping magazine is also available digitally, via the inflight entertainment system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s obviously a tough time for many airlines around the globe, given the impact that higher jet fuel prices are having on economics, in an industry with razor thin margins. Along those lines, German airline Condor is looking for all kinds of way to save on fuel costs… including reducing the number of inflight magazines onboard!

    It has been revealed that aeroTELEGRAPH flags how as of November 1, 2026, German airline Condor has slashed the number of inflight shopping magazines it has onboard flights. Instead of each passenger having their own inflight shopping magazine:.

    Sources indicate that the airline has confirmed that the goal is “to reduce the weight on board and thus fuel consumption,” and it’s pointed out how the inflight shopping magazine is also available digitally, via the inflight entertainment system. These inflight shopping magazines have both the food & drinks available for purchase, as well as duty free items.

    Initially this is being viewed as a trial, and after winter, the airline will decide whether or not to continue with this policy.

    Over the years, we’ve seen a good number of airlines eliminate duty free sales and inflight magazines, with the primary motivation being to reduce the weight of the aircraft. However, it’s definitely a bit unusual to see an airline put a magazine at some seats, but not others. After all, some people may prefer a physical magazine, so are you supposed to ask your seat mate if you can borrow it, or how does that work?!

    In a recent development, I am curious if this leads to a reduction in onboard sales. After all, passengers onboard flights are a pretty captive audience, and might browse a magazine out of boredom. I mean, just look at SkyMall, in all of its former glory. Did anyone really need the world’s largest wine glass, or a bigfoot garden statue? Nope! But if you’re bored enough, you might be convinced of some pretty wild things!

    Recent findings suggest that condor isn’t stopping at inflight magazines when it comes to trying to find ways to reduce the weight of aircraft. This is part of a larger project at the airline, with the goal of operating flights as efficiently as possible, with as much resource conservation as possible.

    In order to find additional cost saving measures, the airline is undergoing a cabin clearing process, as it’s described. This involves removing all movable items from the aircraft, inspecting them, and then deciding if they’re needed anymore. Of course safety equipment is the one exception.

    Industry observers note that realistically, I can’t imagine there’s all that much that can be removed anymore, without cutting some very basic amenities on long haul flights. After all, it’s not the 1970s, and it’s not like there are endless amenities onboard for passengers.

    German airline Condor is asking passengers to share inflight shopping magazines, as part of an initiative intended to reduce the weight of aircraft. While it goes without saying that a single magazine doesn’t lead to a huge increase in fuel burn, when you multiply it by the number of magazines, the number of flights an aircraft makes, and the number of aircraft in the fleet, it sure can add up.

    While eliminating things like seat back magazines is nothing fresh, the concept of sharing magazines is a new one for me. Obviously Condor wants it both ways — it still wants to be able to make money selling things, but doesn’t want the weight of one magazine per person.

    I am curious if this test proves successful, or if this leads to a material reduction in sales.

    What’s your take on Condor’s cost saving initiative?

There is no shopping given it’s a ULCC not the monthly magazine is one that I like forward to whenever boarding an Indigo flight in India.

    • Sources indicate that the carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Alaska Airlines will drop four destinations from its network in Portland, Oregon.

    Sources indicate that the carrier confirmed it will end service from Portland to Baltimore, St. Louis, Upcoming Orleans, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

    Three of the connections launched only months ago. Portland-Jackson Hole came online in June, and service to Baltimore and St. Louis started in May.

    In a recent development, “As we add fresh routes to our network, we constantly assess existing routes to ensure we’re using our aircraft in the markets our guests want most,” the carrier remarked in a statement provided to AirlineGeeks. “As part of that process, we’ve made the decision to discontinue service between Portland and Baltimore, Jackson Hole, St. Louis, and New Orleans. We remain committed to Portland and will continue to invest in opportunities that strengthen our network there, including adding service in markets where we see the greatest opportunities for our guests.”.

    Alaska serves over 60 destinations from Portland, and recently opened a newly introduced lounge there.

    • I’m incredibly fortunate that I’ve never had a “traditional” job — I started OMAAT my freshmen year of college as a hobby (after having been passionate about miles & points in my teens), and nearly 19 years later, that’s still what I get to do full time.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that it’s a substantial day here at OMAAT, as I’m delighted to welcome our first full time contributor in the site’s nearly 19-year history. Let me start with a little bit of background, and then I’ll talk about Daniel Ross, who is joining the team. As a creature of habit, this feels like a whole newly introduced frontier, but I’m excited!

    I’m incredibly fortunate that I’ve never had a “traditional” job — I started OMAAT my freshmen year of college as a hobby (after having been passionate about miles & points in my teens), and nearly 19 years later, that’s still what I get to do full time.

    I’m blessed that I can wake up every day and cover an industry that I love. While OMAAT is a business that pays my bills, it has never been exclusively about maximizing profitability, coming up with some five-year business plan, or seeing what opportunities there are to sell. It’s also my hobby.

    Now, the downside to this — at least if you ask my family — is that I also “work” seven days per week, 365 days per year. Other sites in the space that are this size might have one or two dozen contributors, but for me, that has never sounded very appealing. My passion is actually getting to cover the industry, rather than managing a huge group of people.

    Recent findings suggest that let me be clear, I don’t do this alone, as I have two great people who do a ton of to work to handle everything in the background, much of which readers don’t see — Jeremy oversees business development (basically anything having to do with the business side of things), and Howie manages things related to credit cards and tech (which largely helps pay the bills!). I’m incredibly grateful for their contributions, because it allows me to focus on content.

    Industry observers note that in the past, I’ve had some part time contributors, and I also very much appreciate the contributions they’ve made. However, given the volume of content at OMAAT, it’s hard for that to make a meaningful difference in terms of workload, etc.

    Recently I finally accepted the fact that it’s time to add a full time contributor. That’s not because I want to meaningfully change anything about the site in terms of the content mix, or because I want to step back from things. Quite to the contrary, it’s because I want to do the best possible job I can.

    As many people can surely attest to, if you take pride in what you do (rather than just turning your site into an AI slop machine), it just takes a lot more effort than in the past to accomplish the same results, given how everything on the internet has shifted. Aside from spending time with family, this site and industry is basically my entire life — it’s not a means to an end, but the passion as such is the “end.”.

    So my hope is that by having someone join the team full time on the content front, I can actually put more time into the areas that I’d like to improve — engaging with the community, responding to comments and emails, etc. These are all things I’ve gotten very bad at, not due to a lack of caring, but due to a lack of hours in the day, especially as someone who has two small kids.

    For that matter, I’m planning on imminently launching a new video series (which I wrote about over the summer), not to replace written content, but to complement it, as I think we have a unique angle for it. I just couldn’t carve out the time for that without getting some more help. So I’m finally no longer putting this off, and I’m ripping the band aid-off.

    Recent findings suggest that let me emphasize that the goal here is to genuinely do a better job of providing useful and interesting content to community members, rather than anything else. This isn’t a “we’re cutting free food & drinks in economy due to customer feedback, it’s an enhancement” situation!

    I’d like to welcome Daniel Ross to OMAAT, as he’s joining full time as of today! Daniel isn’t new to the miles & points world, as has he contributed to many sites over the years (The Points Guy, Business Insider, Upgraded Points, etc.), so odds are good that you may be familiar with him (and you can follow him at cometravelwithdan on Instagram).

    Shortly Daniel will be publishing his first post introducing himself, but let me provide a little background on how this came to be, and how I envision this evolving.

    I’ve actually never met Daniel before in person. I’ve always had respect for his work and think he has done a great job with writing, social media, video content, etc. We hadn’t connected until not that long ago, and hit it off.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to working with people, and especially adding them to the OMAAT team, I try to follow my gut, and I think Daniel will be a good fit. I know OMAAT readers value opinions, analysis, and someone with interesting takes, and I think Daniel checks all those boxes. For example, he was just telling me about Aerolineas Argentinas’ quirky baggage allowance, so I’m excited for the expanded content coverage, as that’s something I would’ve never written about (I’m more into covering Air Côte d’Ivoire’s insane first class carry-on allowance).

    One of the specific reasons I don’t want a dozen contributors is because I think it’s notable for people to have a unique voice, and for readers to get to know that, and I think people will enjoy hearing Daniel’s takes on things.

    Industry observers note that daniel also does a great job with social media and video content, which is something that I’ve historically struggled with. My general philosophy is that if I can’t do something right, I won’t do it at all, and that basically sums up the OMAAT strategy for social media up until now. 😉 I think Daniel strikes the unique balance of being interesting without being obnoxious and clickbaity, and I appreciate that.

    According to recent reports, so, what exactly will Daniel be doing at OMAAT? This is very much a “we’re going to evolve together on this” situation, given the initiatives I’ve had in mind for some time:.

    It has been revealed that transparency is vital to me, and Daniel is someone who understands how “particular” the OMAAT community is. 😉 Obviously the OMAAT community is very much about written content, so that’s why I think it’s important that this is where he focuses to begin with, since that’s the medium people are most familiar with. Then we’ll see where things go from there….

    It’s an exciting (scary?) day here at OMAAT, as Daniel Ross is joining the team, as the first full time contributor of the site in its nearly 19 year history. I’m excited, and the goal is to add someone with a unique and interesting voice, to expand coverage on things, etc.

    My hope is also that it frees up a little more time for me, so I can focus a bit more on the community aspect of things. In the long run, you can also expect a bit more of a focus on video and social media, but we’re starting with what we know here!

    Recent findings suggest that I’m excited about this, and Daniel will have a post soon introducing himself. Thanks to everyone for their patience, and stay tuned!

    According to recent reports, PS: For those wondering about the British Airways 747 featured image, it’s because I noticed Daniel had that as his model plane in the background behind his desk during our video calls, so we’ll throw him that Easter egg. 😉.

    #30612. How Are Hotels Paid When You Redeem Points, And For Elite Perks?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1640 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    How Are Hotels Paid When You Redeem Points, And For Elite Perks?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that there’s a real thrill to redeeming points for stays at luxury properties, and getting outsized value.
    • The major global hotel groups (Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Marriott, etc.) don’t own a vast majority of their properties.
    • In some cases, large investment firms own hotels, and they may have properties belonging to all kinds of brands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that there’s a real thrill to redeeming points for stays at luxury properties, and getting outsized value. I’m sure many people have wondered about the economics of that. How much is the hotel getting reimbursed for your stay? Who is paying for any elite perks that you receive? Does the hotel care if you redeemed points or not? Let’s talk about those various points in this post….

    The major global hotel groups (Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Marriott, etc.) don’t own a vast majority of their properties. Instead, the companies have an asset light strategy, and have management or franchise contracts for the individual properties.

    In some cases, large investment firms own hotels, and they may have properties belonging to all kinds of brands. In other cases, a hotel may even be family owned.

    Industry observers note that the way the major hotel groups make money is primarily through fees (they’re also increasingly directly monetizing their loyalty programs, but that’s a whole different topic). There’s typically an initial fee to open the hotel, and then on top of that, there are fees on ongoing revenue. The ongoing fees typically fall into one of two categories (and they’re typically a percentage of revenue):.

    Industry observers note that then any upside (or downside) typically falls with the hotel owner. So the major hotel groups are making money, regardless of whether a hotel is raking in the cash or hemorrhaging money.

    In a recent development, now, one of the reasons that consumers flock to certain hotel groups is because of their loyalty programs, which are massive marketing machines. A significant part of the value proposition of these loyalty programs is the ability to redeem points.

    Industry observers note that as you’d expect, those points are redeemed centrally through the program, and then the loyalty program has to “buy” that room from the hotel. After all, the hotel owner wants to be compensated for each head in a bed, especially since they’re already paying a system fund fee, to fund these perks. That brings us to the question of how hotels are reimbursed….

    Industry observers note that as you’d expect, hotel groups don’t publicly disclose how they reimburse their properties when members redeem points. However, over the years we’ve been able to get some insights into this.

    Sometimes guests are given folios that are actually intended for the loyalty program, while in other cases the reimbursement rates showed up online when they weren’t supposed to.

    While the exact reimbursement policies differ by program, here’s the general concept:.

    So I’m totally making this up here, but if a hotel is charging $400 on a particular night, maybe the loyalty program would pay $80 for that room if occupancy is under 90%, while it might be paying $350 if occupancy is over 90%.

    Industry observers note that note that the number of points you redeem for a stay doesn’t directly determine reimbursement for a hotel. In other words, a hotel doesn’t get paid X amount per redeemed point. Similarly, if a program offers a fifth night free on award redemptions, the hotel is getting reimbursed for all five nights, as it’s the loyalty program incurring the cost there.

    In a recent development, instead, points redemption rates are set by the loyalty program, and are intended to reflect the cost incurred by the program. That’s why in many cases you’ll find that redemption rates don’t correlate directly to how much a property would cost in cash, but rather also factor in average occupancy at a property.

    In a recent development, A hotel loyalty program would probably rather you redeem your points at a $1,000 per night hotel that’s 50% full, rather than a $500 per night hotel that’s 95% full, because the latter redemption will cost the program more. Hotel loyalty programs use historical data to determine points pricing, and the costs they incur.

    Let me actually give a real example from a recent stay. I recently redeemed points for a two night stay at a Wyndham Rewards property, at the cost of 30,000 points per night. The folio I was sent accidentally had the amount Wyndham had to pay, rather than the amount I had to pay.

    Even though I was paying the same number of points both nights, the hotel was being reimbursed around $87 for one night, and $184 for the next night. Funny enough, while sitting in the lobby working the first morning, I overheard one front desk agent tell the other that they were fully sold out the following night, so that tracks. The first night was being reimbursed at a reduced rate, while the second night was being reimbursed based on something closer to the average daily rate.

    It has been revealed that if you have elite status with a hotel loyalty program, how does taking advantage of elite perks factor into this when redeeming points? Who pays for breakfast? Who pays for suite upgrades? Who pays for waived destination fees and parking?

    The answer is that “it depends,” though here are a few general considerations:.

    As you can see, funding elite benefits is a combined effort between the loyalty program and hotels.

    For those curious, generally individual hotels don’t know how you earned your elite status. So it doesn’t matter to them if you earned it through actual hotel stays, or just by holding onto a credit card. Presumably a front desk agent could look at your stay history, but they typically wouldn’t have any reason to do so, in this context.

    This is a loaded question, and there’s obviously no single right or wrong answers. A few thoughts, though.

    Hotel staff are trained by corporate to treat guests redeeming points the same way as those paying cash. Many hotel groups even train front desk staff to thank people for redeeming their points, since it reflects engagement in the program. Officially, you should expect exactly the same treatment as if you paid cash, and you absolutely shouldn’t feel sheepish about the fact that you didn’t pay cash for your stay.

    Industry observers note that now, in practice that might not always be how things play out. There’s sometimes a back and forth between hotel owners and hotel groups. Hotel owners often want it both ways — they want the power of the major hotel group distribution channels and loyalty programs, without actually incurring the costs associated with it, whether it’s complimentary upgrades, points redemptions, or a decent breakfast.

    Will you sometimes find a hotel that’s perhaps a bit condescending if you redeem points and have an glitch? Absolutely, but it’s not how it should be, and it’s the exception rather than the norm. Some may remember my stay at the Aegon Mykonos, at the time a Marriott Autograph Collection property (the hotel has since… mysteriously disappeared?).

    Long story short, I was downgraded despite using a confirmed upgrade, and the manager was completely unapologetic about it, and was unwilling to do anything meaningful. One of his defenses was that I was staying “complimentary,” and therefore shouldn’t be complaining.

    The hotel industry is complex, given the various parties involved, from the hotel group to the individual hotel owners. Hopefully the above is a useful rundown of how reimbursement works when redeeming points. The important thing to understand is that hotels get paid a lot more when you’re redeeming points if the property is full.

    When redeeming points, you definitely shouldn’t feel sheepish about it. You earned your stay, and the reason hotels belonging to major loyalty programs are able to command a revenue premium is because of the points and loyalty perks they offer.

    What’s your take on how hotels are reimbursed for award stays? And do you feel like you’ve ever been treated differently when redeeming points?
